title: Prestroke and Poststroke Physical Activity and Depression, Anxiety, and Fatigue After Ischemic Stroke: A Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Depression, anxiety, and fatigue are common and disabling long-term sequelae of stroke. Whether habitual physical activity before stroke and engagement in physical activity during recovery are associated with poststroke psychological outcomes remains incompletely understood. We investigated associations between physical activity patterns and psychological outcomes during the first year after ischemic stroke.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, consecutive patients with ischemic stroke enrolled in the STROKE-CARD Registry were assessed for depression, anxiety, and fatigue at either 3- or 12-month follow-up after stroke using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale and Fatigue Severity Scale. Physical activity was assessed before and after stroke with the Baecke Questionnaire. Associations between physical activity and psychological outcomes were assessed using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, prestroke and poststroke disability, stroke severity and localization, thrombolysis, prestroke depression, and cognitive impairment.
RESULTS: Within 1050 patients (median age, 70 years; 35% female), 35.3% were screened positive for depression, 29.9% for anxiety, and 53.2% for fatigue at either 3 or 12 months after stroke. Both prestroke and poststroke physical activity were associated with lower odds of depression (adjusted odds ratio, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.36-0.62] and 0.45 [95% CI, 0.34-0.59]; P<0.001) and fatigue (adjusted odds ratio, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.38-0.64] and 0.49 [95% CI, 0.38-0.64]; P<0.001), and with lower odds of anxiety (adjusted odds ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.57-1.00]; P=0.050) and (adjusted odds ratio, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.53-0.94]; P=0.016). High-intensity and high-volume activities were associated with the lowest prevalence of depression and fatigue (depression, 24.5%-25.7%; fatigue, 40.8%-44.1%). Endurance sports were associated with lower rates of depression (22.2%; P<0.001) and fatigue (40.6%; P<0.001), whereas strength training was associated with lower anxiety (12.8%; P=0.003).
CONCLUSIONS: Physical activity before and after stroke was associated with lower odds of depression, anxiety, and fatigue. These findings identify physical activity as a potentially modifiable behavioral factor associated with psychological well-being after stroke and support further evaluation in intervention studies.

title: Quadriceps and hamstring tendon autografts show similar clinical outcomes but distinct strength-recovery profiles after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A meta-analysis.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Graft choice remains a central controversy in primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Quadriceps tendon (QT) and hamstring tendon (HT) autografts may provided similar clinical outcomes but differ in donor-site morbidity and postoperative strength recovery.
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether QT and HT autografts differ in patient-reported outcomes, knee stability, functional performance, strength recovery, donor-site morbidity, and safety after primary ACLR.
EVIDENCE REVIEW: PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from inception to March 17, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) directly comparing QT and HT autografts. The protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD420261340928). Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. No external funding was received.
FINDINGS: Fifteen RCTs involving 936 participants were included, with 470 participants receiving QT autografts and 466 receiving HT autografts. Mean ages ranged from 18.7 to 32.7 years, and most studies reported follow-up at 12 or 24 months. At 24 months, no statistically significant differences were detected between QT and HT autografts in IKDC score (MD = -1.19; 95% CI, -3.84 to 1.47; p = 0.38), Lysholm score (MD = 1.42; 95% CI, -0.60 to 3.45; p = 0.17), or Tegner score (MD = -0.15; 95% CI, -0.70 to 0.39; p = 0.58). At the final available follow-up, graft failure occurred in 12 of 265 participants (4.5%) in the QT group and 11 of 261 participants (4.2%) in the HT group, without a statistically significant difference (RR = 1.11; 95% CI, 0.49 to 2.48; p = 0.81). Overall adverse events also showed no statistically significant difference (RR = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.45 to 1.11; p = 0.13). QT autografts were associated with lower donor-site morbidity scores at 24 months (MD = -4.62; 95% CI, -9.21 to -0.03; p = 0.048), although this secondary finding was based on two trials. Knee stability, range of motion, return-to-sport, and hop-test outcomes showed no consistent differences. At 12 months, HT autografts were associated with relatively greater quadriceps strength symmetry, whereas QT autografts were associated with relatively greater hamstring strength symmetry and higher hamstring-to-quadriceps (H/Q) strength ratios.
- CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: QT and HT autografts produced similar patient-reported, stability, return-to-sport, and safety outcomes after primary ACLR but demonstrated distinct graft-specific strength-recovery profiles. These findings support individualized graft selection rather than consistent clinical superiority of either graft.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, systematic review, and meta-analysis of RCTs.

title: Effectiveness of Digital Health Interventions on Rehabilitation Outcomes in Patients After Total Knee Arthroplasty: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is the most effective treatment for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, but some patients continue to experience persistent postoperative pain, stiffness, and impaired functional recovery. Digital health interventions are increasingly used in rehabilitation after TKA, but their comparative effectiveness remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different digital health interventions on rehabilitation outcomes in patients after TKA and to compare and rank these interventions in terms of pain relief, active knee flexion range of motion (ROM), and knee function to provide evidence for selecting optimal rehabilitation strategies.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Google Scholar, Scopus, CINAHL, MEDLINE (via OvidSP), CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) meeting the inclusion criteria. The RoB 2 tool (Risk of Bias 2; Cochrane) was used to assess risk of bias, and the confidence in network meta-analysis (CINeMA) framework was used to evaluate certainty of evidence. Traditional meta-analysis and network meta-analysis (NMA) were performed using Stata (version 17.0; StataCorp LLC). A random-effects model (DerSimonian-Laird method for estimating τ²) was consistently used across all analyses. For outcomes measured with the same or convertible scales, mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were used to pool effect sizes. Surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values were calculated to summarize the ranking probabilities.
RESULTS: A total of 36 RCTs involving 3067 patients after TKA were included. NMA results showed that compared with conventional rehabilitation (CR), for active flexion ROM, rehabilitation robot (RR; MD 8.96, 95% CI 5.86-12.05), mobile app-based telerehabilitation (MAT; MD 6.36, 95% CI 2.81-9.91), and virtual reality (VR; MD 5.92, 95% CI 2.94-8.90) were significantly superior to CR; for the Hospital for Special Surgery knee score, VR (MD 9.53, 95% CI 5.18-13.88), intelligent rehabilitation system-based telerehabilitation (MD 6.90, 95% CI 2.35-11.44), and RR (MD 5.32, 95% CI 1.61-9.04) were significantly superior to CR; for pain, RR and MAT had relatively high ranking probabilities, but the 95% CIs of most comparisons included 0; for the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index and Timed Up and Go test, only internet videoconference-based telerehabilitation and VR-based telerehabilitation, respectively, were significantly superior to CR. The certainty of evidence for most comparisons was low or very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Digital health interventions may improve pain, active knee flexion ROM, and knee function in patients after TKA. In the SUCRA ranking, RR, VR, and MAT showed favorable ranking probabilities; however, because the network was predominantly star-shaped and the rankings were derived largely from indirect comparisons, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive. Further high-quality studies with direct head-to-head comparisons are needed.

title: Neurocognitive Alterations Manifested as Reaction Time Deficits Following ACL Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is associated with changes in cognitive-motor processing that may persist beyond physical recovery and are not fully identified by conventional physical performance assessments.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate neurocognitive function as expressed through cognitive-motor performance following ACLR compared with healthy individuals, with particular emphasis on reaction time and higher-order cognitive outcomes.
METHODS: Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase) were searched from inception to December 2025. Eligibility criteria included observational studies on cognitive-motor outcomes in individuals from ACLR recovery and healthy controls. Data extraction followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools. Random-effects models were used to calculate standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2, subgroup analyses and publication bias evaluations.
RESULTS: Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participants Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participantswere included. Neurocognitive performance showed a significant impairment in reaction time from ACLR recovery with a moderate effect size (standardized mean difference = 0.56, 95% confidence interval 0.41-0.71, p < 0.001) and high heterogeneity (I2 = 78%). In contrast, pooled analyses showed no statistically significant differences for error rate, accuracy, visual memory, or visual motor speed.
CONCLUSIONS: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with persistent reaction time deficits, whereas pooled analyses of error rate, accuracy, visual memory, and visual motor speed did not demonstrate statistically significant differences compared with healthy controls. This pattern suggests selective impairment in the temporal efficiency of cognitive-motor processing rather than generalized cognitive dysfunction. Reaction time may represent a potential marker of altered cognitive-motor processing following ACLR; however, prospective studies are needed to determine its prognostic value and clinical utility for post-ACLR assessment and return-to-sport decision making.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation Versus Blood Flow Restriction Alone: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Blood flow restriction (BFR) training is increasingly combined with neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) in musculoskeletal rehabilitation to augment strength and hypertrophy, but whether NMES adds benefit beyond BFR alone remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared combined BFR + NMES with BFR alone for muscle strength, muscle morphology (mass, thickness, cross-sectional area), neuromuscular activation, and functional performance. Methods: Randomized trials comparing simultaneous BFR + NMES with BFR alone were eligible. MEDLINE via PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Google Scholar were searched from inception through 15 September 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data; risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE. Random-effects meta-analysis was restricted to independent parallel-group comparisons; crossover and limb-randomized results were pooled only when paired effect estimates and variances were available, otherwise synthesized narratively. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251076162). Results: Five randomized trials involving 174 participants were included. The studies represented healthy-participant training, experimental limb disuse, acute physiological responses, and low-load training in football players with knee osteoarthritis. Quantitative synthesis of torque-based strength found no clear difference between BFR + NMES and BFR alone (MD -41.78 Nm, 95% CI -396.68 to 313.12; p = 0.375; 2 trials, 52 participants), with substantial statistical heterogeneity. Cross-sectional area and rectus femoris EMG RMS were each reported by only two trials and were synthesized narratively. Certainty of evidence was very low across all outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence does not establish a consistent additional benefit of adding NMES to BFR. The pooled torque-based estimate is exploratory because of the small evidence base, substantial statistical heterogeneity, imprecision, and differences in clinical context and outcome measurement. A possible effect on preserving muscle mass during short-term experimental disuse remains preliminary. None of the included trials directly investigated BFR + NMES following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), and its effectiveness in this population remains undetermined.

title: Comparative effects of motor-control interventions on neuromuscular and biomechanical outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuromuscular-control and biomechanical deficits may persist after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Comparative motor-control effects remain uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: To compare motor-control interventions after ACLR.
DESIGN: Systematic review and network meta-analysis.
METHOD: Seven databases were searched to 12 May 2026. Usual rehabilitation comprised conventional symptom control, motion, strengthening, gait, or functional training. Three neuromuscular-control outcomes underwent network meta-analysis; k ≥ 2 biomechanical comparisons were pooled and k = 1 estimates unpooled. RoB 2 assessed bias; CINeMA and GRADE assessed confidence.
RESULTS: Thirty-two trials enrolled 1437 participants. Proprioceptive training improved joint position sense versus usual rehabilitation (SMD 1.02, 95% CI 0.54-1.50; moderate CINeMA confidence); jump-landing control training yielded a favorable dynamic-balance estimate versus usual rehabilitation (1.19, 0.59-1.80; low CINeMA confidence) and was sensitive to exclusion of a late-phase multi-arm athlete trial; feedback-enhanced (0.88, 0.43-1.32) and proprioceptive training (0.59, 0.21-0.97) favored postural control (both low CINeMA confidence). Pooled estimates suggested that neuromuscular training may improve knee valgus and knee flexion kinematics during single-leg landing (1.51, 0.51-2.51; 1.07, 0.49-1.65); pooled gait biomechanical symmetry was inconclusive (-0.41, -0.87-0.05). Across networks, τ² ranged from 0.0275 to 0.1698; global tests detected no statistically clear inconsistency (P = 0.087-0.229), although sparse loop structures limited inference.
CONCLUSION: Moderate-confidence evidence supported proprioceptive training for improving joint position sense after ACLR. Other interventions may help balance and landing control, but their benefits are less certain. The evidence does not establish a single best approach across outcomes.

title: Effects of dietary nitrate supplementation in team sport athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dietary nitrate (NO3 -), typically provided as beetroot juice, increases nitric oxide availability and may reduce the oxygen cost of exercise, improve muscle oxygenation, and delay fatigue. Evidence in team sport athletes, however, remains limited and has not been comprehensively synthesized. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluate the effects of NO3 - supplementation on team sport-specific performance and related physiological and biochemical outcomes.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42022358739). PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through March 2025 for randomized, placebo-controlled trials investigating acute (single dose) or chronic (≥2 days, with the final dose taken 2-3 h before exercise) NO3 - supplementation in male or female team sport athletes. Effect sizes (Hedges' g) were synthesized using multilevel random-effects models (REML) with cluster-robust standard errors. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.0 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Robustness analyses, including sensitivity to assumed within-person correlations for crossover trials and Monte Carlo simulations to examine the stability of key contrasts under sparse evidence were performed.
RESULTS: Twenty-four trials (n = 365 athletes; 277 males, 88 females) met inclusion criteria. Supplementation increased circulating and salivary NO3 -/NO2 -, indicating elevated systemic concentrations. The overall pooled ergogenic effect on performance was small but statistically significant (g = 0.075; 95% CI 0.026-0.124; p = 0.005). In team sport-specific tasks, NO3 - supplementation produced a small but consistent improvement with low heterogeneity and moderate certainty of evidence (g = 0.143; 95% CI 0.041-0.245; p = 0.011). A significant benefit was observed with chronic protocols (g = 0.145; 95% CI 0.076-0.214; p < 0.001), whereas acute protocols showed no clear effects. The chronic-acute contrast was statistically significant (g = 0.118; 95% CI 0.029-0.207; p = 0.013) but was not robust to more conservative crossover-correlation assumptions, lowering certainty to very low; because chronic protocols also included a final pre-exercise dose, this contrast should not be interpreted as evidence of long-term adaptation. Improvements were most evident in team sport-specific performance tests (moderate certainty), with additional, less certain signals in repeated high-intensity efforts and fatigue-sensitive neuromuscular outcomes (both very low certainty), while single-sprint outcomes and most metabolic/biochemical markers showed no consistent benefit. Cardiorespiratory responses were largely unchanged. Dose-response meta-regressions did not reveal consistent linear or non-linear trends.
CONCLUSIONS: NO3 - supplementation provides small, context-dependent ergogenic benefits in team sport athletes, most consistently for team sport-specific performance (moderate certainty), with preliminary signals for repeated high-intensity efforts and fatigue-sensitive neuromuscular performance (both very low certainty). Evidence for moderation by protocol type, sex, and training status remains suggestive but uncertain and is currently insufficient to support specific dosing recommendations. Well-powered, standardized, sex-stratified trials with harmonized outcome measures are needed to clarify key moderators and strengthen applied guidance.

title: Network meta-analysis of the efficacy of different exercise therapies in patients with knee osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability in the elderly and a growing social burden due to aging and increasing obesity rates. This study aims to investigate the effects of different exercise modalities on pain, physical function, stiffness, and muscle strength in patients with KOA.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and EBSCO databases for randomized controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of exercise therapy for KOA from January 2000 to 16 August 2025, followed by an updated search through 28 March 2026. No additional eligible studies were identified in the updated search. In total, 51 studies involving 3,045 participants (71.7% female; study-group mean ages ranged from 50.3 to 74.4 years) were included. The studies were conducted in 14 countries across Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania. A network meta-analysis was performed using Stata 16.0. This systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251177632).
RESULTS: The results showed that mind-body exercise was the most effective in reducing pain (standardized mean differences (SMD) = -1.13, 95% confidence interval (CI) [-1.47 to -0.79], P < 0.001, Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA) = 83%) and improving joint stiffness (SMD = -1.15, 95% CI [-1.59 to -0.70], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 78.5%). Mixed exercise ranked highest in improving knee function (SMD = -1.43, 95% CI [-2.31 to -0.55], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 81.8%), followed by mind-body exercise (SMD = -1.28, 95% CI [-1.64 to -0.93], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 77.4%). Strength training was most effective in enhancing muscle strength (SMD = 0.79, 95% CI [0.470-1.12], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 79.1%).
CONCLUSION: Mind-body exercise appeared to be the most favorable option for reducing pain and stiffness in patients with knee osteoarthritis, whereas strength training appeared to be the most beneficial for improving muscle strength. These findings may help inform individualized exercise prescription, but should be interpreted cautiously given the uncertainty and limitations of the available evidence.

title: Comparative Effects of Different Neuromuscular Training Modalities and Doses on Lower-Limb Injury Prevention in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lower-limb injuries are common in athletes. Neuromuscular training (NMT) is widely promoted, but the comparative effectiveness of different modalities and the optimal dose remain uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted a PRISMA-compliant, PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library and Embase were searched to 1 August 2025. Eligible trials compared NMT with a control in athletes and reported lower-limb injury outcomes. Random-effects models pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Two reviewers screened, extracted and assessed risk of bias. Prespecified subgroups examined modality and dose (frequency, session duration, intervention length), age, sex and sport. Certainty was rated with GRADE.
RESULTS: Twenty-seven RCTs (27,663 participants) were included. NMT was associated with reduced lower-limb injury risk (RR = 0.72, 95% CI 0.64-0.82), although trim-and-fill adjustment attenuated the estimate. Structured (RR = 0.68, 95% CI 0.56-0.82) and multidimensional programmes (RR = 0.76, 95% CI 0.61-0.93) showed favourable pooled estimates, with no statistically significant between-modality difference. Favourable pooled estimates were also observed in adolescents (RR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.81) and young adults (RR = 0.70, 95% CI 0.50-0.99), and in football (RR = 0.71) and basketball (RR = 0.66); however, the between-age difference did not remain statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, and no statistically significant differences were detected between sport subgroups. Low-certainty, study-level subgroup analyses yielded favourable pooled estimates for programmes delivered 2-3 times per week, for 16-25 min per session, and over intervention periods of 1.5-12 months; however, these associations did not establish a causal or optimal dose. Certainty was very low overall and low to very low across dosage comparisons.
CONCLUSIONS: NMT may reduce lower-limb injury risk, but the magnitude of benefit remains very uncertain. Structured and multidimensional programmes, together with programmes delivered at moderate frequency and duration, showed favourable pooled estimates in exploratory subgroup analyses; however, the dose-related findings represent study-level associations and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal or optimal dose. These findings may inform the design of routine training programmes, while future high-quality RCTs should address adherence, long-term sustainability, and dose-response interactions across sports and populations.

title: The addition of remplissage to arthroscopic labral repair is associated with lower rates of recurrent instability and higher rates of return to sport for patients with on-track Hill-Sachs lesions: a systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative studies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite being initially described for off-track Hill-Sachs lesions (HSLs), the addition of remplissage to arthroscopic labral repair (ALR) for on-track HSL continues to generate significant interest. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to evaluate outcomes for ALR with and without remplissage for on-track HSL.
METHODS: A preregistered Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was performed using PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL from database inception until October 23, 2025. Inclusion criteria were comparative studies for ALR with remplissage (ALR + R group) vs. ALR alone without remplissage (ALR group) for on-track HSL. Primary outcomes included recurrent instability events, return to sport, and revision surgery. A random effects meta-analysis with relative risk (RR) was conducted.
RESULTS: Eight articles were included out of 170 retrieved. Patients (n = 928; mean age: 24.0 years; 79.1% male; follow-up: 33.5 months; distance-to-dislocation: 14.2 mm; Hill-Sachs interval: 9.6 mm; percent of glenoid bone loss: 3.8%) were stratified into ALR + R (n = 298) and ALR (n = 630) groups. ALR + R patients had a 72% lower risk of recurrent instability events compared to ALR patients (RR: 0.28; P < .001; 3.4% vs. 16.0%). Among contact athletes only, the recurrent instability rate was 2.0% (n = 1) in the ALR + R group (n = 50) and 16.7% (n = 9) in the ALR group (n = 54). There was a statistically significant 15% higher risk of return to sport in the ALR + R group as compared to patients in the ALR group (RR: 1.15; P = .003; 76.3% vs. 68.9%). There was no difference in revision rates for the ALR + R group despite a greater than 4-fold higher revision rate in the ALR group (P = .08; 1.6% vs. 7.4%). Certainty of evidence for all analyses was "very low" due to the quality of evidence.
CONCLUSION: The addition of remplissage to ALR for on-track HSL appears to have clinically and statistically significant benefits for reducing the risk of post-operative recurrent instability events as well as promoting higher rates of return to sport, despite very low certainty of evidence. Future randomized controlled trials are needed for corroboration.

title: Effects of velocity-based strength training versus percentage-based strength training on technical error rates in collegiate lion dance athletes: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lion dance is a Chinese intangible cultural heritage that demands exceptional strength, explosive power, and movement precision. Velocity-based training has shown benefits for general athletic performance, but its effects on sport-specific technical performance in traditional sports remain unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the effects of velocity-based training and percentage-based training on technical error rates in collegiate lion dance athletes.
METHODS: Thirty collegiate lion dance athletes were recruited and randomly assigned in fixed head-tail pairs to a velocity-based training group (VBT, n = 10), a percentage-based training group (PBT, n = 10), or a regular-training control group (CON, n = 10). Both training groups completed a 6-week intervention (3 sessions per week) consisting of back squats (tail athletes) and strict overhead presses (head athletes). The VBT group used real-time velocity feedback with a 10% velocity-loss threshold; the PBT group followed a progressive percentage-based loading protocol (50-70% 1RM). All three groups continued the team's regular lion dance technical and conditioning training. Two blinded assessors evaluated sitting-on-shoulder and standing-on-leg technical error rates weekly. The unit of analysis for both primary technical outcomes was the head-tail pair (n = 5 pairs per group; 15 pairs total). Maximal strength (squat 1RM, strict press 1RM) was measured at baseline and post-intervention as a secondary outcome. The principal between-group analyses were analysis of covariance at each follow-up time point with the baseline error rate as covariate, supported by a 3 × 7 mixed-design repeated-measures ANOVA evaluating the Group × Time interaction. Significance testing of baseline imbalances among randomized groups was not performed, in accordance with current methodological recommendations.
RESULTS: All 30 participants completed the intervention. Statistically significant Group × Time interactions were found for both sitting-on-shoulder (F(12, 72) = 1.99, P = 0.037, partial η2 = 0.249) and standing-on-leg (F(12, 72) = 4.24, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.414) error rates. ANCOVA-adjusted between-group comparisons indicated that the VBT group reduced sitting-on-shoulder error rate significantly more than the CON group from Week 3 onward and significantly more than the PBT group from Week 5 (adjusted mean difference at Week 6 vs CON: -35.5 percentage points, 95% CI: -50.6 to -20.4; vs PBT: -19.5 percentage points, 95% CI: -34.6 to -4.4). The corresponding pattern was observed for standing-on-leg error rate (adjusted mean difference at Week 6 vs CON: -36.0 percentage points, 95% CI: -48.6 to -23.4; vs PBT: -18.4 percentage points, 95% CI: -31.2 to -5.7). For secondary maximal-strength outcomes, the Group × Time interactions were statistically significant for both squat 1RM (F(4, 24) = 14.47, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.707) and strict press 1RM (F(4, 24) = 9.45, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.612). Post-hoc analyses showed that VBT and PBT produced significantly larger pre-to-post 1RM gains than CON; VBT and PBT differed marginally on squat (mean difference +2.72 kg, P = 0.049) and not significantly on strict press (+0.70 kg, P = 0.706).
CONCLUSION: Among these collegiate lion-dance athletes, velocity-based training produced significantly greater between-group reductions in sitting-on-shoulder and standing-on-leg error rates than continued regular lion-dance training alone, and a significantly greater reduction than percentage-based training from the fifth week of the intervention. Both strength-training regimens produced significantly larger maximal-strength gains than continued regular training, but VBT and PBT were largely comparable in strength gains despite VBT's substantially greater technical advantage over PBT, suggesting that the technical-performance advantage of velocity-based training is not adequately explained by between-method differences in maximal-strength gains. Larger, multi-center trials are needed to confirm these preliminary findings.

title: Maximal Aerobic Capacity and Aging in Female Masters Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Maximal aerobic capacity ( V ˙ O2max) represents the highest rate at which the body can use oxygen during intense exercise and is a key determinant of endurance performance. Although age-related declines in V ˙ O2max have been well documented in male individuals, less is known about this trajectory in female Masters athletes, defined as individuals aged 40 years or older who often engage in lifelong endurance training.
OBJECTIVE: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify cross-sectional age-related differences in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes.
METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 14 May, 2025 for studies reporting directly measured V ˙ O2max in female Masters endurance athletes aged 40 years or older. Eligible exercise modalities included running, cycling, swimming, and large muscle-mass ergometry, with testing conducted under standard environmental conditions. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using a modified Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled mean V ˙ O2max values were calculated for predefined age groups (40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70 years or older) using a random-effects meta-analysis. Meta-regression was used to estimate the relationship between age and V ˙ O2max.
RESULTS: Sixty-nine studies, including 1903 female Masters athletes, met the inclusion criteria. Pooled mean relative V ˙ O2max was 45 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 43.0-46.8) in athletes aged 40-49 years, 40 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 38.5-41.7) in those aged 50-59 years, 35 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 33.2-37.1) in those aged 60-69 years, and 30 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 27.2-31.8) in athletes aged 70 years or older. Meta-regression demonstrated that each additional year of age was associated with a 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 lower V ˙ O2max (95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.44; P < 0.0001), equivalent to about 11.7% per decade. The association was consistent across testing modalities.
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrates a progressive age-related decrease in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes. Maximal aerobic capacity declines at an average rate of 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 per year after age 40 years, corresponding to approximately 11.7% per decade. This decline is evident across endurance sport disciplines and appears consistent with physiological changes associated with aging despite sustained endurance training. These findings provide female-specific reference values and a quantitative framework for future studies on aerobic capacity trajectories in female athletes.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S2RXZ ).

title: Lower-limb performance and muscle soreness after short-term dark chocolate intake in CrossFit®-trained women: an exploratory secondary analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dark chocolate (DC) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for exercise performance and recovery, but evidence in trained women remains limited. This exploratory secondary analysis examined selected lower-limb performance outcomes and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) in female CrossFit® athletes.
METHODS: This secondary analysis included 15 trained female CrossFit® athletes from a randomized crossover trial. No separate a priori sample-size calculation was performed for these outcomes (minimum detectable paired effect, d_z = 0.78). DC (30 g/day, 85% cocoa), placebo chocolate (PLA), and an open-label control (CONN) were compared at four operationally defined menstrual-cycle assessments after three days of supplementation. DC-PLA allocation was blinded, but blinding success was not assessed. Outcomes were vertical jump height (VJH), knee isokinetic and isometric performance, and muscle-specific DOMS after the Cindy WOD.
RESULTS: Condition effects survived FDR control for VJH and 19 of 22 dynamometry outcomes. Across assessments, VJH was 34.48 ± 5.09 cm with DC and 30.22 ± 2.34 cm with PLA (mean difference 4.27 cm, 95% CI 1.45 to 7.08; Holm-adjusted p = 0.017; g_av = 1.09). No condition-by-assessment interaction survived FDR control (all q ≥ 0.141). DOMS showed significant time effects for all three muscles, peaked at approximately 24 h, remained elevated at 48 h, and declined toward baseline by 72 h. A condition-by-time effect remained significant only for gastrocnemius soreness (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012; ηp2 = 0.212); no DOMS condition main effect or condition-by-assessment-by-time interaction was supported.
CONCLUSION: DC was associated with higher values for selected lower-limb outcomes, but these exploratory findings do not establish phase-specific efficacy, equivalent effects across cycle assessments, or a consistent DOMS benefit. Unusually large performance estimates and unmodeled period and carryover effects warrant caution.

title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up).
RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months.
CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.

title: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation combined with resistance exercise for knee osteoarthritis: randomized clinical trial protocol.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Resistance exercise is the gold-standard conservative treatment for knee osteoarthritis (KOA). However, arthrogenic muscle inhibition and quadriceps weakness may limit the effectiveness of strengthening programs. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) has been proposed as an adjunct strategy to enhance muscle activation, yet current evidence in KOA remains inconclusive and methodologically limited.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effects of adding NMES, applied concurrently with voluntary contractions, to a resistance exercise program in individuals with KOA.
METHODS: This double-blind, parallel-group randomized controlled trial will include 84 participants with clinically diagnosed KOA, randomly allocated (1:1) to resistance exercise combined with either active or sham NMES. Both groups will perform supervised sessions twice weekly for eight weeks. The primary outcome will be knee pain assessed by the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Secondary outcomes will include self-reported physical function, knee extensor torque, performance-based physical function, and adverse events. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, post-intervention, and 12-week follow-up. Data will be analyzed using linear mixed models under the intention-to-treat principle.
CONCLUSION: This study may clarify whether adding NMES provides additional therapeutic benefits in KOA rehabilitation and support evidence-based clinical decision-making.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ensaiosclinicos.gov.br identifier is RBR-77f8rjq.

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

title: Multi-planar patellar hypomobility as a potential contributor to VMO-VL dyssynergy and return to sport limitations following ACL reconstruction in soccer players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patellofemoral hypomobility (PFH) is a frequent yet underestimated complication following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. PFH induces biomechanical and neuromuscular alterations that impair return to sport (RTS) and accelerate early joint degeneration. However, current evidence describes PFH primarily as an associated factor rather than a direct causal determinant of RTS failure. Therefore, the primary objective of this review is to analyze the correlation between PFH and functional complications during RTS. The study also aims to summarize the available evidence on the relationship between PFH and medium- to long-term clinical outcomes, without implying causal predictions where not supported.
METHODS: A narrative review was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science using a Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO)-structured search. No systematic review procedures or pooled quantitative analyses were performed; all numerical data derived from individual studies. Included studies involved athletes aged 18-35 undergoing primary ACL reconstruction with Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone (BPTB) or Hamstring autografts.
RESULTS: The analysis reveals significant PFH (>25% compared to the contralateral side) in 15-22% of athletes at 6 months, with a peak of 28% in BPTB graft cases. Longitudinal hypomobility correlates with extension deficit, whereas transverse hypomobility is associated with increased anterior knee pain (AKP) in 34% of cases. Data indicate a 12-15% reduction in Countermovement Jump (CMJ) performance and a 3.4-fold higher risk of patellofemoral osteoarthritis (PFOA) within 5 years, although PFH was not directly measured as an independent variable in these studies. Additionally, 25% of athletes with PFH discontinue competitive activity within 36 months after RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: PFH emerges as an important factor associated with postoperative functional limitations. Restricted patellar glide disrupts the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO)/vastus lateralis (VL) synergy, reduces performance, and accelerates cartilage degeneration. Symmetry of patellar kinematics should be considered a relevant parameter for RTS decision-making, while acknowledging that RTS outcomes are multifactorial and not solely determined by PFH.

title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Relationship between global functional outcomes and patient-reported instability after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction: A midterm case series of 292 patients.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate midterm patient-reported outcomes, return to sport (RTS) rates and instability-specific symptoms after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction (AALALR), and to evaluate the relationship between global functional recovery and perceived ankle stability.
METHODS: We retrospectively analysed 292 patients who underwent AALALR between January 2015 and May 2022, with a mean follow-up of 4.9 ± 1.8 years. Global outcomes were assessed using the foot and ankle ability measure (FAAM) and simple ankle value (SAV), while instability-specific perception was evaluated with the French Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT-F). RTS, satisfaction and complications were also recorded. No objective postoperative laxity assessment was performed.
RESULTS: Mean FAAM-ADL was 94.3 ± 12.0, FAAM-Sports 87.5 ± 20.4 and SAV 85.1 ± 17.4; 89.7% of patients returned to sport and 91.1% were satisfied. Overall, 104 patients (35.6%; 95% CI, 30.3-41.3) met the CAIT-F criterion for instability at follow-up (score ≤23/30). Patients with CAIT-F-defined instability had significantly lower FAAM and SAV scores and RTS rates (all p < 0.001), although most had returned to sport (79.8%) and were satisfied (81.7%). The CAIT-F correlated moderately with FAAM-activities of daily living (ADL), FAAM-Sports and SAV (Spearman ρ = 0.68-0.69) and receiver operating characteristic analysis showed imperfect agreement between global scores and CAIT-F-defined categories (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.82-0.85). The reoperation rate was 5.5%.
CONCLUSION: AALALR provides high midterm satisfaction, favourable functional scores and favourable RTS rates. However, over one-third of patients reported current CAIT-F-defined instability symptoms. Global and instability-specific instruments are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable, and prospective studies including objective laxity assessment are needed.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, case series.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male (first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women.
CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention strategies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Recovery of Running and Technical Match Performance After Adductor Muscle Strain Injury in Male Professional Football Players: A Prospective Cohort Study of 27 Players From One LaLiga Team Across Five Seasons.
abstract: Post return-to-play (RTP) running and technical match performance after adductor muscle strain injury remains unclear. The aim of the present study was to examine recovery of running and technical match performance after RTP following acute adductor muscle strain injury in professional football. This prospective longitudinal cohort study followed players from one team (n = 122) across five seasons (2020/2021-2024/2025). Injuries were recorded by the medical staff and confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging. Match performance variables included playing time, total distance, high-speed running distance (> 24 km/h), number of sprints (> 24 km/h), and offensive and defensive technical actions. First eight matches following RTP were compared with the four pre-injury matches. RTP required unrestricted team training and medical clearance for match selection. Data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations methods, adjusting event counts for the amount of playing time. Of the 122 players, 27 sustained at least one acute adductor muscle strain injury, accounting for 54 injury episodes. At Match 1, time played was -7.1% versus PRE (95% CI -16.7% to +3.5%), total-distance rate -0.4% (-2.4% to +1.5%), high-speed running distance +6.9% (-3.5% to +18.5%), and number of sprints +5.9% (-4.0% to +16.8%); none remained significant after FDR adjustment (p ≥ 0.182; pFDR ≥ 0.817). At Match 8, total passes were 26.5% below PRE (95% CI -50.0% to +7.9%; raw p = 0.116; pFDR = 0.567). Across all Match 1-8 contrasts, only long passes at Match 3 remained significant after FDR adjustment (-15.3%; 95% CI -22.4% to -7.6%; raw p < 0.001; pFDR = 0.022). In conclusion, there was little evidence of systematic population-level impairment in running or technical match performance after RTP. Late passing reductions warrant confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

title: Stress Fracture Recovery and Return to Sports in Youth with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare stress fracture recovery times in children with and without juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), and to evaluate JIA-related factors associated with recovery.
STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective case-control study included children with JIA <19 years old with a first stress fracture treated at a single center from 2004-2024. Cases were matched 1:3 to children without JIA by age, gender, and fracture location. Recovery time was defined from imaging confirmation of a stress fracture to medical clearance to return to sports. We used a generalized estimating equations method to compare recovery times and evaluate associations with JIA-related factors, including JIA subtype, glucocorticoid and arthritis-directed therapy exposure, and proximity of arthritis to fracture location.
RESULTS: The cohort included 260 children (65 cases, 195 controls; 53.8% female; median age 14.3 years [IQR 12.6, 16.2]). Pars interarticularis fractures accounted for 30.8% of injuries, followed by metatarsal (23.1%), and tibial fractures (14.2%). Among children with JIA who sustained pars fractures, 75.0% had an enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA) phenotype. Median recovery times were 10.6 (IQR 7.0, 19.4) weeks for children with JIA and 10.6 (IQR 7.1, 14.6) weeks for controls (P=0.197), with no significant differences for lower-extremity fractures. In contrast, children with JIA who sustained pars fractures had longer recovery times than controls (ratio of geometric means: 1.44, 95% CI 1.01, 2.05; P=0.045). Among children with active sacroiliitis, fractures occurred more frequently in the proximate pars or pelvis than at non-proximate sites (P<0.001). Recovery time was not associated with JIA subtype (all p>0.150), glucocorticoid exposure (P=0.365), or biologic therapy (P=0.625).
CONCLUSIONS: Overall recovery times did not differ significantly between children with and without JIA. However, children with JIA and pars fractures had longer recovery times, and associations with ERA and sacroiliitis warrant further investigation. Additional research on spondylolysis recovery in young athletes with JIA may help inform individualized return-to-sports recommendations.

title: Bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with a higher 1-year risk of thigh muscle injury after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in competitive male athletes: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft type and subsequent thigh muscle injury in athletes involved in pivoting sports.
METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted on 221 ACLRs performed in 199 competitive male athletes involved in pivoting sports, classified according to graft donor site: extensor mechanism (bone-patellar tendon-bone [BPTB] or quadriceps tendon) and flexor mechanism (hamstring tendon). Only athletes who returned to sport and completed a minimum of 12 months of follow-up were included. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed thigh muscle injuries occurring within the first year following the discharge date were identified and classified by muscle group injured and graft type.
RESULTS: Thirty-five athletes (15.8%) sustained at least one MRI-confirmed thigh muscle injury (41 muscle-group-level injuries in total) in the year after discharge from ACLR. Athletes who received a graft from the extensor mechanism had a higher proportion of any thigh muscle injury than those with hamstring grafts (27/133, 20.3% vs. 8/88, 9.1%; absolute risk difference 11.2%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.4-20.0; odds ratio [OR] 2.45, 95% CI 1.12-5.88; p = 0.037). Muscle-group analyses showed no significant differences for hamstring injury or quadriceps injury. All six adductor injuries occurred in the extensor donor group (4.5% vs. 0%), but this difference was not statistically robust. After adjustment, none of the three muscle-group comparisons remained significant.
CONCLUSION: Extensor mechanism grafts were associated with a higher proportion of athletes sustaining any thigh muscle injury in the year following discharge from rehabilitation; although absolute rates were low, no individual muscle group showed a significant difference.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players.
HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41).
CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

title: Long-term market value decline after medial collateral ligament injury in professional football players did not differ statistically significantly from matched non-injured controls: A Transfermarkt-based cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to characterize the longitudinal trajectory of estimated market value after medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury in professional football players and determine whether postinjury changes differed from matched non-injured controls.
METHODS: Professional football players with a recorded MCL injury were identified from Transfermarkt injury records labeled as medial (collateral) ligament injuries (seasons 2007/08-2023/24); duplicate records of the same episode were merged, and injuries were not clinically verified. Market value was assessed during the season preceding injury (Tpre), the injury season (T0), and annually for five subsequent seasons (T1-T5). Linear mixed-effect models evaluated longitudinal changes and associations with age, playing position, league level, and injury-related absence. Segmented models assessed changes in temporal trajectory. MCL cases were also matched 1:2 to non-injured controls by competition, season, playing position, age, and preinjury market value, with group differences examined using a difference-in-differences model.
RESULTS: Forty-five players with 50 MCL injury episodes were included, 8 of which had an associated anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal lesion. Median age at injury was 26.5 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 23.0-28.7), and median time lost was 42 days (IQR: 21-76.5). In the adjusted model, market value did not differ statistically significantly from Tpre at T0 (P = 0.649), T1 (P = 0.813), or T2 (P = 0.064) but was statistically significantly lower at T3 (-34.25%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -51.21% to -11.38%; P = 0.006), T4 (-47.54%; 95% CI: -61.54% to -28.43%; P < 0.001), and T5 (-51.70%; 95% CI: -65.25% to -32.88%; P < 0.001). No statistically significant postinjury change in slope was observed (P = 0.103). Thirty-one of 48 eligible cases were matched to 62 controls; the remaining 17 had no eligible control within the matching criteria, mostly because of lower-tier competition or low preinjury market value. Difference-in-differences estimates were not statistically significant at any time point (P = 0.167-0.561; range: -10.9% [95% CI: -39.2% to 30.6%] at T0 to -24.6% [95% CI: -49.5% to 12.6%] at T3); the study could detect only differences of approximately 42%-46% or more. Results were unchanged when analyses were restricted to isolated MCL injuries.
CONCLUSIONS: Market value declined substantially during long-term follow-up after MCL injury, but this decline was not statistically significantly different from that observed in matched non-injured players (P = 0.167-0.561). Much of the apparent long-term depreciation may therefore reflect the underlying age- and career-related trajectory of professional footballers; however, the matched analysis was underpowered, and a modest injury-specific effect, particularly after more severe injuries with longer absence, cannot be excluded. Because injury grade and treatment were unavailable, these findings should not be generalized to high-grade or operatively treated MCL injuries.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Minimally Invasive Surgery for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy Using a Double-Row SpeedBridge Repair with Rip-Stop Augmentation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The present video article describes a minimally invasive surgery (MIS) technique utilizing a double-row rip-stop SpeedBridge (Arthrex) repair for the treatment of insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT). This procedure is utilized when nonoperative treatment has failed, with the goal of returning patients to their previous levels of activity while avoiding the complications associated with more open procedures. All products mentioned in the videos are manufactured by Arthrex.
DESCRIPTION: The surgical technique is performed with 4 small incisions-2 distal and 2 proximal. Any Haglund deformity and/or enthesophyte are resected with use of an MIS burr through the 2 distal portals. The central third of the Achilles tendon is partially detached with this resection and is repaired with use of a double-row repair. Proximal anchors are placed, and sutures are passed through the Achilles tendon. Working knotless sutures are tensioned to create a rip-stop suture. The sutures are passed and shuttled to the distal row, creating a double-row repair. The distal row is drilled and tapped. The double-row repair is completed with insertion of distal anchors under appropriate tension.
ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative treatment is beneficial in the initial stages of the condition and is successful in 60% to 80% of patients1-3. Initial treatment strategies for IAT include RICE (rest, ice, compression, and elevation), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy. Eccentric exercise and extracorporeal shockwave therapy have shown promising results3. Paratendinous injections, such as with platelet-rich plasma, have shown various levels of success and need further evaluation3. When nonoperative treatment has failed, operative treatment is a viable option. The surgical approach should be chosen on a patient-specific basis, as different tendinopathy patterns and different associated osseous and soft-tissue conditions may influence preoperative planning. There are a variety of different surgical techniques that include open, endoscopic, and MIS procedures.
RATIONALE: This MIS technique utilizing a double-row SpeedBridge repair with rip-stop augmentation yields fewer wound complications, less pain, quicker initiation of rehabilitation protocols, and quicker return to sport compared with more invasive techniques. Furthermore, the addition of the rip-stop augment to the double-row SpeedBridge repair improves dynamic mechanical strength and mitigates suture tearing through the tendon4.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: In our experience, patients who undergo this technique will be weight-bearing in a controlled-ankle-motion boot immediately postoperatively and out of the boot by 6 weeks postoperatively, with progressive return to full activities as tolerated. Our study of 61 patients undergoing the double-row SpeedBridge repair demonstrated favorable outcomes, with Foot and Ankle Disability Index scores improving from a mean of 56.3 preoperatively to 98.62 at 12 months postoperatively and visual analog scale pain scores improving from a mean of 7.25 to 0.476. There were no postoperative ruptures at a mean follow-up of 12.5 months. Eleven patients had minor complications within 3 months, including 6 who reported some central numbness over the Achilles tendon6. We expect these outcomes to improve as surgeons become more comfortable and skilled performing MIS techniques.
IMPORTANT TIPS: Proper patient selection (chronic IAT with Haglund deformity and/or an enthesophyte) will help ensure optimal outcomes.It is important to develop a subcutaneous plane for suture passage.The use of fluoroscopy or a nanoscope is helpful in ensuring that the proper bone is resected with the MIS burr.We have found that the irrigator from the MIS burr can be utilized alongside a Frazier suction tip to help remove excess bone.Suture management is important. Precisely maneuver the sutures at all times; it is very important that the sutures do not get tangled so that the procedure flows efficiently.Make sure to fully tension both sutures in order to place the ripstop.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugMRI = magnetic resonance imagingK-wire = Kirschner wireCI = confidence intervalBID = twice dailyprn = as neededDVT = deep vein thrombosis.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: STUDY00004409).

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

title: Patients treated with rehabilitation alone after anterior cruciate ligament injury display greater muscle strength symmetry, yet lower absolute muscle strength normalized to bodyweight compared to reconstruction: A Cross-sectional study of 3,093 patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Younger patients active at a greater activity level are in general treated with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) while older, less active patients receive rehabilitation alone as primary treatment. Objective of this study was to compare muscle strength, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) between patients treated with rehabilitation alone and rehabilitation with additional ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during the first 12 months after treatment.
DESIGN: Registry-based cohort study.
SETTING: Cross-sectional comparisons adjusted for age and sex using ANCOVA.
PARTICIPANTS: 3093 patients (2707 ACLR; 386 rehabilitation), aged ≥15 years and registered in Project ACL.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Muscle strength and PROs assessed at 10 weeks, 4, 8, and 12 months after ACL injury or ACLR.
RESULTS: In the comparison between patients treated with rehabilitation alone and ACLR, patients in the rehabilitation alone group had greater muscle strength symmetry at all follow-ups but lower absolute strength normalized to bodyweight in the uninjured limb, except hamstrings strength at 10 weeks. Patients in the rehabilitation group reported higher KOOS symptoms at 8- and 12 months and sports/recreation at 10 weeks, present K-SES18 was higher at 10 weeks but lower at 12 months, while future K-SES18 was lower at all follow-ups. Patients in the rehabilitation alone group reported lower ACL-RSI was lower at 12 months and Tegner activity levels were lower pre-injury and at all follow-ups.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients treated with rehabilitation alone had greater symmetrical strength, but lower uninjured limb absolute strength normalized to bodyweight compared to patients treated with ACLR. Patients in the rehabilitation alone group also reported less knee symptoms, but inferior present and future knee self-efficacy compared with patients treated with ACLR.
