title: Arthroscopic Stabilization Reduces Recurrence but May Delay Return to Sport After First-Time Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocation in Elite Male Athletes: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management for first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation in adult athletes, with a focus on recurrent instability, return-to-play rates, and time to return to play.
METHODS: Five databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Studies comparing arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management in adult athletes (≥18 years) with first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation were included. The primary outcome was recurrent instability. Secondary outcomes included return-to-play rates and time to return to play. A narrative synthesis was performed given the nonrandomized and heterogeneous nature of included studies. Evidence certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation.
RESULTS: Five studies (232 participants: 111 operative, 121 nonoperative) were included. Recurrent instability rates ranged from 3% to 14% in the operative group and 24% to 80% in the nonoperative group. Return-to-play rates were high for both approaches (operative: 93%-100%; nonoperative: 97%-100%). Nonoperative management was associated with earlier return to sport (2.3-5.7 weeks vs 18.7-39.3 weeks for operative management in studies reporting this outcome). All studies involved elite athletes, with female athletes substantially under-represented.
CONCLUSIONS: Arthroscopic stabilization was consistently associated with lower rates of recurrent instability than nonoperative management after first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation but required a longer time to return to play. Nonoperative management enabled an earlier return to play but was associated with higher recurrence. The evidence is limited primarily to male military, collegiate, and professional athletes, restricting generalizability to female, recreational, and broader adult athletic populations.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.
METHODS: In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.
RESULTS: EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: -10.9%, 95%CI: -21.4;-0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: -9.80, 95%CI: -18.3;-1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.
CONCLUSION: n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

title: Influence of ballistic and conventional resistance training on bone properties in postmenopausal women: A randomised controlled trial.
abstract: High-load conventional resistance training (CRT) is recommended for osteoporosis prevention. Ballistic resistance training (BRT) involves high velocity and impact forces with lower loads. The Resistance Exercise Programme on Risk of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis in Females (REPROOF) study examined effects of BRT and CRT, relative to control (CON) on proximal femur BMD. Healthy postmenopausal women aged 50-70 years were randomised into BRT, CRT or CON groups. BRT and CRT conducted supervised resistance training twice weekly for eight months. In CRT, concentric and eccentric phases each lasted ~2 s at 55-80% of one-repetition maximum (1RM). BRT involved explosive (maximum velocity) concentric movements at 20-50% of 1RM. Proximal femur and lumbar spine BMD were measured by DXA; tibia structure by peripheral QCT. Groups were compared using ANCOVA, adjusting for baseline values. Of 109 women randomised, 82 (63.1 ± 3.7 years; 24.5 ± 3.5 kgm-2; femoral neck T-score -1.1 ± 0.8) completed the study, with 98% adherence. BRT improved total hip BMD (+0.008 [0.001, 0.014] g/cm2; P = 0.02) versus CON. CRT did not affect hip BMD but tibial shaft cortical BMD increased (+4.141 [1.007, 7.274] g/cm2; P = 0.01) and cortical thickness declined relative to CON (-0.07 [-0.13, -0.01] mm; P = 0.03), accompanied by tibial shaft widening. BRT increased total hip and trochanter BMD (P ≤ 0.03) in the subgroup with low BMD. BRT benefitted proximal femur BMD relative to CON, including in the subgroup with low BMD. CRT did not affect hip BMD but caused tibial shaft structural adaptation that may affect strength in bending. BRT based interventions should be further developed and evaluated for osteoporosis prevention.

title: Characterising the Internal and External Load During Warm-Up, Match Play and Training in Soccer Substitutes: A Systematic Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Shorter match-play exposure for soccer substitutes relative to those who start matches has implications in the days before, during and following match play concerning their training, preparatory and recovery/compensatory practices. Specifically, characterising the internal and external loading of substitute players throughout a weekly microcycle can facilitate evidence-based recommendations aimed at optimising their performance readiness.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic scoping review aimed to map and characterise the internal and external loading associated with warm-up, match play and training in soccer substitutes.
METHODS: Prior to literature searches being conducted, a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) statement was formed. Online database (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science) searches were performed according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) protocols. Studies were eligible if internal or external characteristics of soccer substitutes were measured in training or match-play scenarios. After calibration exercises, two authors independently quality assessed each study, with Cohen's kappa undertaken to assess inter-rater agreement. A scoping review methodology was selected because of the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity across studies, which precluded meaningful meta-analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 5135 studies were identified, 66 of which met study criteria. Substantive inter-rater agreement was observed (κ = 0.939, p < 0.001) during the quality assessment of included studies. Soccer substitutes' body temperature, and thus several aspects of physical performance, may not be maintained at time of pitch entry (body temperature pre-pitch entry ~ 37 °C vs match play > 38 °C). Substitutes may experience lower absolute physical loading during training and match day (e.g. match-day 'top up' activity: ~ 17 min; total distance: ~ 1700 m) but during match play, substitutes typically cover higher relative total distances (~ 109 to ~ 137 m·min-1), high-speed running (~ 9.8 to ~ 13.5 m·min-1) and sprinting distance (~ 3.8 to 5.0 m·min-1) compared with players who started the match. Substitutes playing in the second-half exhibit increased heart rates compared with full-match players (84% vs 81% maximum heart rate); however, this remains lower than the first-half heart rate responses of full-match players (84% vs 86% maximum heart rate).
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic scoping review summarises current evidence and key findings relating to the internal and external characteristics of soccer substitutes during warm-up, match play and training that can be used in practice to inform player welfare and sport science support within these cohorts. Chiefly, during match-day warm-ups, soccer substitutes' body temperature and physical performance responses may not be maintained, despite typical substitute-specific match-day practices being employed. Similarly, soccer substitutes were frequently reported to demonstrate higher relative total distance, high-speed running and sprinting outputs compared with starting players. Further research is needed to better understand performance demands, longitudinal adaptations, contextual influences and female-specific responses in soccer substitutes.

title: Lower extremity joint biomechanics from a single crossover drop task demonstrate superior predictive potential for secondary ACL injuries than drop vertical jump or single leg landing tasks.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Secondary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a significant concern after return-to-sport (RTS) following ACL reconstruction (ACLR), with rates as high as 24%. Identifying biomechanical predictors of re-injury is critical for improving RTS protocols.
PURPOSE: To compare the predictive potential of three common landing tasks [drop vertical jump (DVJ), single-leg landing (SLL), and single-leg crossover drop (SCD)] for secondary ACL injury risk in post-ACLR athletes.
METHODS: A multicenter cohort of 150 athletes (age 13-30 years) that were cleared for RTS post-ACLR completed DVJ, SLL, and SCD tasks during 3D motion analysis; 144 athletes data met criteria for analysis. Peak kinematic and kinetic variables (n = 126) were analyzed using a penalized logistic regression with an elastic net penalty. Predictive models were evaluated via ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values.
RESULTS: The SCD task demonstrated the strongest predictive performance for secondary ACL injury, with a validated positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.57, negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96, sensitivity of 80.0%, specificity of 88.9%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.933. The DVJ demonstrated moderate predictive performance (PPV=0.43, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=85.7%, AUC=0.843), while the SLL demonstrated the lowest performance (PPV=0.33, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=78.6%, AUC=0.736).
CONCLUSION: Lower extremity biomechanics during SCD provide greater predictive performance for secondary ACL injury compared with the DVJ or SLL. The findings suggest that SCD captures biomechanical characteristics relevant to secondary ACL injury risk and may improve identification of athletes at elevated risk following ACL reconstruction. However, further validation and model simplification are needed before clinical implementation as a stand-alone screening tool.

title: Five-year outcomes after brace-free versus brace-based rehabilitation following isolated anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft: long-term follow-up of a randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Postoperative knee bracing following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains common practice despite growing evidence questioning its clinical benefit. Previous studies demonstrated that brace-free rehabilitation was noninferior to brace-based rehabilitation one year after isolated ACLR using hamstring tendon autograft; however, its long-term effects remain unknown. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term effects five years after surgery.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients enrolled in a prospective randomized controlled trial conducted between 2016 and 2019 were recontacted approximately five years after isolated primary ACLR with hamstring tendon autograft for a long-term follow-up. In the original trial, 139 patients had been randomized to postoperative rehabilitation without a brace (n = 71) or with a functional knee brace (n = 68). Participants completed several patient-reported outcome measures. Furthermore, a standardized telephone interview was performed. Changes between the one-year and five-year follow-up were analyzed.
RESULTS: Ninety-seven patients participated in the long-term follow-up (n = 45 brace-free group, n = 52 brace group). Mean follow-up was 5.2 ± 1.0 years. No significant differences were observed between groups regarding subjective knee function, activity level, quality of life, rerupture rate, revision surgery, or persistent knee-related complaints at final follow-up. However, there was a significant interaction between treatment group and time for the subjective IKDC score. Patients treated without postoperative bracing showed stable or slightly improved subjective knee function, whereas patients treated with a brace demonstrated a significant decline between one and five years.
DISCUSSION: Brace-free rehabilitation after isolated ACL reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft remains safe and effective more than five years after surgery. Postoperative bracing did not reduce rerupture rates, revision surgery, or long-term functional impairment. Instead, brace-free rehabilitation demonstrated a more favorable longitudinal development of subjective knee function. These findings further question the routine postoperative prescription of rehabilitative knee braces following isolated ACL reconstruction.

title: Earlier and More Criteria-Based Return to Sport After Pediatric Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in North America Compared With the Asia-Pacific Region: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the management and rehabilitation strategies for pediatric anterior cruciate ligament injuries between North America and the Asia-Pacific region.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library was performed for studies published between January 2020 and August 2025. Articles were included if they described pediatric anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation protocols for patients 18 years and younger. Included studies consisted primarily of retrospective studies, cohort studies, case series, technical notes, and cross-sectional studies (Levels II-IV). Data were extracted on bracing use and duration, weight-bearing status, range-of-motion restrictions, sports progression, and return-to-sport criteria.
RESULTS: Forty studies were included (27 North America, 13 Asia-Pacific). Bracing was used frequently in both North America (86%) and Asia-Pacific (72%), with North American protocols often specifying duration (2-6 weeks) or criteria-based discontinuation, whereas Asia-Pacific protocols frequently omitted details. Early range-of-motion restoration was advocated in both regions (North America 85%, Asia-Pacific 91%), although restrictions were applied when meniscal repair was performed. Both regions supported early weight-bearing regardless of surgical technique. Both regions shared similar timelines for running and jogging restrictions; however, North American centers (60%) introduced sport-specific drills earlier between 3 and 6 months. Return-to-sport clearance was delayed beyond 9 months in most protocols (North America 46%, Asia-Pacific 62%). North American center, however, showed more flexibility with 46% allowing return-to-sport clearance before 9 months. North American centers more often incorporated functional criteria (50%) alongside time-based measures, whereas Asia-Pacific centers relied primarily on time-based thresholds.
CONCLUSIONS: Early rehabilitation protocols after pediatric anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction were similar between North America and the Asia-Pacific region with respect to bracing, weight-bearing, and range-of-motion practices. However, return-to-sport progression differed because North American centers more frequently introduced sport-specific activities earlier and more commonly incorporated functional criteria in addition to time-based thresholds, whereas Asia-Pacific centers more often relied on time-based clearance and delayed sport-specific progression.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV evidence.

title: Train hard, recover smart: the supplement framework to enhance exercise recovery in recreational and elite-level athletes.
abstract: Background: Exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage are frequent consequences of structured physical activity that facilitate muscle growth and subsequent training adaptations. Performance improvements are strongly dependent upon athletes' capacity to successfully recover from previous sessions or challenging efforts, particularly when opportunities to rest and recover are limited. Nutritional practices centered around acute or chronic ingestion of certain foods or dietary bioactive compounds have been shown to accelerate neurophysiological and subjective recovery outcomes and may be worthy of consideration in both recreationally active and professional athletic populations. Methods: This review provides a comprehensive summary of dietary strategies to promote exercise recovery that are supported by robust scientific evidence, including systematic reviews, randomized clinical trials, and observational studies up to August 2025. Results: Despite substantial variability in evidence quality, identified nutrients, dietary supplements, and bioactive compounds of greatest interest for athletes are omega-3 fatty acids and creatine monohydrate, while additional compounds showing promising results in improving subjective or objective recovery metrics such as inflammatory biomarkers, muscle soreness, and fatigue include magnesium, taurine, curcumin, L-Carnitine, Ashwagandha, anthocyanins, L-Citrulline, gingerol, tart cherry, beetroot, and pomegranate juice. Nutrients or compounds often popularized but requiring further investigation, current research gaps, and methodological limitations within the available body of literature are also discussed. Conclusion: The findings outlined in this review may inform evidence-based recovery nutrition strategies for both elite and recreational athletes.

title: Musculoskeletal injury epidemiology among football players in Africa: A systematic review of injury incidence, patterns and associated factors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Football is widely played across Africa, yet evidence on the epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries among African football players remains fragmented across countries, populations, and competitive settings. Differences in injury definitions, surveillance methods, and exposure measurement further limit comparison between studies. This systematic review synthesised the available evidence on musculoskeletal injury epidemiology in African football.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database, and Google Scholar were systematically searched from inception to the final search date, supplemented by backward citation searching. Studies investigating musculoskeletal injuries among football players in Africa were eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Methodological quality and risk of bias were evaluated using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tools, as appropriate. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-six studies were included. Sixteen studies contributed 18 incidence estimates, ranging from 2.2 to 289 injuries per 1,000 athlete-exposure hours, while 10 studies reported prevalence estimates ranging from 4.1% to 81.6%. Tournament surveillance studies generally reported higher incidence than season-long studies, and match incidence exceeded training incidence where both were reported. Lower-extremity injuries predominated, particularly at the ankle and knee, while sprains or ligament injuries, contusions, and muscle-related injuries were the most frequently reported injury types. Previous injury or recurrence was the most consistently identified associated factor.
CONCLUSION: Musculoskeletal injuries are common in African football, but substantial methodological heterogeneity limits direct comparison of estimates. Standardised injury surveillance and stronger prospective research are needed to improve the evidence base and support context-specific injury prevention.

title: Education and exercise compared to education alone for hip osteoarthritis: Protocol for the EDUEX randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patient education (EDU) and exercise are universally recommended as first-line treatment for hip and knee osteoarthritis (OA). Specifically in hip OA, the evidence that exercise is a necessary addition when comprehensive EDU is delivered is sparse. Additionally, no randomized trial has evaluated effects of exercise on articular cartilage in hip OA assessed by magnetic resonance imaging. This randomized trial will evaluate whether adding progressive resistance training (PRT) to EDU results in superior improvements in 1) patient-reported physical function and 2) collagen integrity of the hip articular cartilage.
METHODS: This multicenter, stratified, block randomized, controlled, parallel-group, efficacy, superiority trial will be conducted at hospitals and physiotherapy clinics in Denmark. A total of 150 people with hip OA will be enrolled and randomized in a 1:1 ratio to only participate in an EDU program or to the same EDU program and additionally 12 months of partly supervised group-based PRT. The primary outcome is between-group difference in change from baseline to 12 months in 1) the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score activities of daily living function subscale for the primary clinical superiority study and 2) T2 relaxation time mapping of the hip articular cartilage for the primary mechanistic superiority study (P-MECH).
DISCUSSION: The EDUEX trial will provide high-quality evidence for assessing the clinical efficacy of adding PRT to EDU in people with hip OA while also assessing the effects on hip articular cartilage.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT06391554.

title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort.
METHODS: Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score).
RESULTS: Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed.
DISCUSSION: Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

title: Targeting Medial Leg Pain in Athletes: Distinguishing Between Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome and Tibialis Posterior Tendinopathy.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To examine the clinical overlap between medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS) and tibialis posterior tendinopathy (TPT) in athletes with exercise-induced medial lower leg pain. Current evidence regarding anatomy, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, imaging, and management is reviewed to improve diagnostic accuracy and highlight emerging concepts regarding posterior tibial tendon (PTT) involvement in athletes traditionally diagnosed with "shin splints."
RECENT FINDINGS: Although MTSS remains the most common diagnosis for exercise-induced medial tibial pain, growing biomechanical and imaging evidence suggests PTT pathology may be more prevalent than previously recognized, particularly in athletic populations. MTSS and TPT share overlapping symptom location, gradual onset, and activity-related pain, contributing to potential misdiagnosis. Despite these similarities, important distinctions exist in physical examination findings, foot biomechanics, imaging characteristics, and treatment strategies. Additionally, evolving concepts surrounding progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD) have better defined the relationship between PTT pathology and medial foot and ankle instability. The broad clinical diagnosis of "shin splints" may encompass a subset of athletes with unrecognized TPT. Careful assessment of PTT function, foot alignment, and lower extremity biomechanics should complement evaluation of medial lower leg pain athletes. Improved recognition of TPT may facilitate earlier diagnosis, guide appropriate rehabilitation, prevent progression to PCFD, and identify opportunities for future prospective studies directly comparing MTSS and TPT in athletic populations.

title: Return to Sport and Clinical Outcomes after Surgical Stabilization of Chronic Ankle Instability in Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) can compromise athletic performance and delay return to competition. Although primary ligament repair and ligament reconstruction are valid surgical options, comparative data remains limited.
PURPOSE: The primary aim was to evaluate overall return-to-sport outcomes after surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability in athletes. The secondary aim was to compare return-to-sport and postoperative clinical outcomes between direct ligament repair and ligament reconstruction.
STUDY DESIGN: Comparative retrospective study METHODS: This comparative cohort study included 54 athletes who underwent surgical stabilization for CAI between 2018 and 2024. Surgical procedures were categorized as primary repair and ligament reconstruction. The primary outcomes were RTS status and time to RTS. Secondary outcomes included postoperative Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) scores and residual complaints.
RESULTS: The mean age was 25.6 ± 6.9 years, and 48% of patients were football players. The median interval from the latest injury to surgery was 6.0 months. RTS status was available for 49 of the 54 athletes (91%). Of these, 48 (98%) returned to sport at a mean time of 5.3 months (range 2.0 to 16.0), while one athlete did not return to sport. Postoperative functional outcomes were favorable, with mean FAAM activities of daily living and sport scores of 96.2 ± 8.3 and 89.7 ± 20.4, respectively. No statistically significant differences were observed among surgical groups in RTS status, time to RTS, FAAM scores, or residual complaints.
CONCLUSION: Surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability was associated with favorable postoperative scores and a high RTS rate among athletes with available outcome data. The sample size and overall study design preclude conclusions regarding the equivalence or superiority of repair versus reconstruction.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: [Research progress on correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament injury and bone bruise].
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To review the research progress on the correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and bone bruise.
METHODS: Relevant literature on non-contact ACL injury and bone bruise published in recent years was reviewed. The imaging characteristics and injury mechanisms of bone bruise, factors affecting bone bruise distribution, the associations between bone bruise and combined intra-articular injuries, and the impact of bone bruise on postoperative outcomes after ACL reconstruction were summarized and analyzed.
RESULTS: Bone bruise is a common MRI finding in non-contact ACL injury, mainly involving the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau. The typical "kissing" bone bruise pattern can reflect the abnormal loading condition of the knee joint at the moment of injury and provides important imaging evidence for inferring the injury mechanism of ACL rupture. The occurrence and distribution of bone bruise may be influenced by factors such as age, osseous morphology of the knee, and meniscal anatomical characteristics. The extent, location, and severity of bone bruise are associated with knee laxity, anterolateral ligament injury, meniscal tears, and articular cartilage injury to varying degrees. Among these, the association between lateral compartment bone bruise and lateral meniscal injury is relatively well established, while bone bruise of the medial tibial plateau may indicate occult posterior horn injury of the medial meniscus. Bone bruise may also be associated with early postoperative pain and recovery of knee range of motion after ACL reconstruction, and may increase the risk of cartilage degeneration and post-traumatic osteoarthritis. However, its predictive value for mid- and long-term knee function and clinical outcomes remains inconclusive.
CONCLUSION: Bone bruise can reflect, to some extent, the loading mechanism and severity of non-contact ACL injury, and provides important clues for identifying associated structural injuries and evaluating prognosis. However, the grading and assessment criteria for bone bruise remain unstandardized, and controversies remain regarding its associations with certain combined injuries and long-term clinical outcomes. Further standardized, large-scale, multi-center, and long-term follow-up studies are required to clarify the clinical value of bone bruise in the assessment and prognostic evaluation of ACL injury.

title: Effects of repeated isometric exercise on pain-related and physical recovery outcomes following exercise-induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate repeated quadriceps isometric exercise for recovery following experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes.
DESIGN: Parallel-group, randomized sham-controlled trial.
METHODS: Forty university athletes were randomized to isometric exercise (n = 20) or sham exercise (n = 20). Co-primary outcomes were pressure pain threshold and soreness intensity; secondary outcomes were knee flexion range of motion, quadriceps isometric strength, and thigh circumference. Assessments occurred before and immediately after soreness induction and on Days 1, 3, and 5. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for soreness (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.898), pressure pain threshold (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.745), and knee flexion range of motion (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.378). Soreness was lower in the isometric group on Day 1 (mean difference, -2.55 points; 95% confidence interval -3.00 to -2.10; Hedges' g = -3.19) and Day 3 (-1.90 points; 95% confidence interval -2.35 to -1.45; Hedges' g = -2.74). Pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed no significant between-group differences at individual time points. Group × Time interactions were not significant for quadriceps strength or thigh circumference.
CONCLUSIONS: Repeated submaximal isometric exercise was associated with lower perceived soreness during peak symptoms. Although pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed different temporal patterns, neither differed significantly between groups at individual time points. Benefits for physical recovery outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Limitations of Rotational Acceleration for Predicting Concussion: A New Injury Risk Function.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Rotational acceleration of the head has long been hypothesized to be a primary driver of concussion because it can generate shear strains in brain tissue, while linear acceleration has been considered less injurious due to the brain's near-incompressibility. Instrumented mouthguards (iMGs) now enable direct six-degree-of-freedom measurements of human concussion, making it possible to rigorously test this hypothesis for the first time in vivo. The purpose of this study was to test the hypothesis that rotational acceleration is a more precise predictor of concussion than linear acceleration using iMG measurements of concussion across a multi-sport dataset.
METHODS: A dataset of 47 concussive and 3,804 non-concussive iMG-measured impacts was compiled across male and female athletes in seven sports. Univariate and bivariate logistic regression models were developed using peak linear acceleration, peak rotational acceleration, and peak rotational velocity to assess concussion classification and contribution to injury risk. Models were evaluated using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), F1 score, and odds ratios. Additionally, a novel liquid-filled helmet technology was evaluated during laboratory impacts using the derived risk functions.
RESULTS: Contrary to our hypothesis, rotational acceleration was not a significantly more precise classifier than linear acceleration (AUPRC = 0.36 vs 0.65; F1 = 0.31 vs 0.50) and was not a significant independent predictor of concussion alongside linear acceleration in a bivariate model (ORrot = 1.3, 95% CI 0.81-1.9; ORlin = 2.3; 95% CI 1.5-3.6). However, peak rotational velocity provided additional predictive value in a bivariate risk function with peak linear acceleration. Applying this bivariate function to laboratory football helmet tests, the liquid-filled padding reduced predicted concussion risk by up to 60% relative to a standard American football helmet, primarily due to attenuating linear acceleration.
CONCLUSION: Rotational acceleration was not a significant independent predictor of concussion and was outperformed by linear acceleration in classification, challenging its primacy in injury risk evaluation. Our results support a broader consideration of linear acceleration and rotational velocity in concussion risk assessment and prevention.

title: Effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation applied simultaneously with exercise therapy in patellofemoral pain: A single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simultaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) during exercise may augment task-specific quadriceps activation, but its additional effects in patellofemoral pain (PFP) are uncertain. This pilot trial examined whether adding simultaneous NMES improved pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, quadriceps strength, and muscle thickness compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation.
METHODS: In this single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial, 30 participants were allocated 1:1 to an intervention group or acontrol group. Both groups received the same hip- and knee-targeted exercise therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks. The intervention group received NMES during leg press and leg extension exercises, whereas the control group wore the same device with stimulation intensity set to zero. The primary outcome was worst pain during the previous week, assessed using the visual analogue scale(VAS). Secondary outcomes included the anterior knee pain scale (AKPS), Y-Balance Test (YBT) composite score, isokinetic quadriceps strength (60°/s, 180°/s), and quadriceps muscle thickness.
RESULTS: No additional between-group benefit was detected for worst pain (p = .96; Cohen's d = -0.03), AKPS (p = .26; Cohen's d = -0.24), YBT composite (p = .28; Cohen's d = -0.26), isokinetic strength at 60°/s (p = .67; Cohen's d = -0.11), or 180°/s (p = .56; Cohen's d = -0.12). Total quadriceps muscle thickness increased more in the intervention group than in the control group, but the effect was small (p = .03; Cohen's d = -0.27). No adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: No additional short-term benefit of adding simultaneous NMES to exercise therapy was detected for pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, or quadriceps strength compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation. A small increase in total quadriceps muscle thickness was detected, but its clinical relevance remains uncertain. These findings do not support routine addition of simultaneous NMES for short-term pain relief or functional improvement.

title: Running Gait Biomechanics Associated With Tibial Bone Stress Injuries Among Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tibial bone stress injuries (BSIs) are common among adolescent runners; however, no studies have evaluated running biomechanics associated with tibial BSI in adolescents.
OBJECTIVE: To describe biomechanical and clinical features among adolescents with a history of tibial BSI, and compare with healthy age- and sex-matched controls.
DESIGN: Retrospective cross-sectional case-control study.
SETTING: Large tertiary-care hospital and affiliated sports injury prevention center.
PARTICIPANTS: Sixty-six adolescents with history of tibial BSI (16.2 ± 1.8 years, BMI: 21.4 ± 3.0 kg/m2) were compared with 66 age- and sex-matched adolescents without a history of tibial BSI (16.3 ± 1.9 years, BMI: 21.7 ± 2.6 kg/m2).
INTERVENTIONS: Medical record review was conducted for tibia BSI case participants. Data from gait analyses completed on an instrumented treadmill.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Participant demographics were compared using independent samples t-tests. Continuous outcome measures [stride length, cadence, %stance phase, and peak mass-normalized vertical ground reaction force (vGRF)], and vertical average load rates (VALR), were compared between groups using independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, with Cohen d effect sizes reported.
RESULTS: Study participants with history of tibial BSI demonstrated increased VALR (μ = 1141, P = 0.01, d = 0.29), increased mass-normalized maximum vGRF (μ = 1657, P = 0.02, d = 0.24), and greater % stance phase (μ = 1392, P < 0.001, d = 0.36).
CONCLUSION: Adolescents with a history of tibial BSI demonstrated characteristic gait biomechanics including greater VALR, greater mass-normalized maximum vGRF, and more terrestrial gait pattern. These features should be considered in management of adolescent tibial BSI.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Design and Repeatability Testing of a Novel Benchtop Apparatus for Evaluating Wear Durability of Artificial Tendons.
abstract: Artificial tendons are potential alternatives to biological grafts for reconstructing large tendon defects, yet their clinical translation is limited partly by mechanical durability during repetitive gliding against pulley-like structures (e.g., retinacula). Standardized methods for evaluating long-term tendon-pulley wear under physiologically relevant conditions are lacking. This study aimed to develop a benchtop testing methodology for mechanical wear of artificial tendons after high-cycle loading. A custom apparatus was designed to simulate key biomechanical features of the flexor pollicis longus tendon, including tensile load, excursion velocity, and wrapping angle at the tendon-pulley interface. Apparatus performance and repeatability were evaluated using polyester tendons subjected to 1.02 million simulated thumb flexions, equivalent to approximately 395 days of simulated physiological thumb motion, at a rate of 22.1 simulated flexions per second. Non-lubricated testing resulted in excessive frictional heating (93 °C within 40,800 simulated thumb flexions), causing premature thermal damage and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) variability. Conversely, applying boundary lubricant at the tendon-pulley interface, mimicking synovial fluid, maintained temperatures at approximately 36 °C and eliminated non-physiological thermal degradation. Under lubricated conditions, wear scar morphology was consistent with isolated mechanical fiber abrasion, and median UTS was 865.7 N (848.0-887.2 N), with high inter-trial repeatability across three independent tests (p = 0.3688). This study establishes a reproducible experimental framework for isolating mechanical wear in artificial tendons under high-cycle gliding and is suited for orthopaedic research applications, including material screening and design optimization of tendon grafts and tendon-implant interfaces.

title: Assessment of Pain and Functional Recovery Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Combined With Secretome Injection.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Predictable graft healing following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction remains a clinical challenge, particularly because insufficient ligamentization and tendon-bone integration may be associated with graft failure and less favorable functional outcomes. Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived secretome represents a cell-free biological approach comprising diverse bioactive molecules with potential regenerative properties, as supported by preclinical studies. This study aimed to compare pain intensity and functional outcomes at six months after ACL reconstruction using a peroneus longus tendon (PLT) autograft, with and without adjunctive intralesional administration of MSC-derived secretome.
METHODS: This study enrolled 24 patients undergoing arthroscopic single-bundle anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using a peroneus longus tendon (PLT) autograft. Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive either an intralesional injection of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived secretome into the graft (secretome group, n = 12) or an equivalent-volume saline placebo (control group, n = 12). Clinical outcomes were assessed preoperatively and at 6 months postoperatively using the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) Subjective Knee Evaluation Form, Tegner-Lysholm Knee Scoring Scale, and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain intensity. Between-group comparisons were conducted using the independent-samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, and followed by ANCOVA analysis as appropriate to the distributional characteristics of the data. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: At baseline, IKDC and VAS scores did not differ significantly between the secretome and control groups (IKDC: 48.57 ± 4.91 vs. 47.51 ± 4.45, p > 0.05; VAS: 7.75 ± 0.62 in both groups, p = 1.000). At the six months follow-up, patients receiving adjunctive secretome injection demonstrated significantly higher IKDC scores than controls (86.89 ± 5.11 vs. 78.27 ± 3.91, p < 0.01). Similarly, Tegner-Lysholm scores were significantly higher in the secretome group (87.08 ± 5.16 vs. 79.33 ± 2.67, p < 0.01). Pain intensity was also significantly lower in the secretome group, as reflected by lower VAS scores (2.17 ± 0.72 vs. 3.92 ± 0.79, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Adjunctive MSC-derived secretome administration during anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using a peroneus longus tendon (PLT) autograft was associated with higher International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective knee scores and Tegner-Lysholm knee scores, as well as lower Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores, at 6 months postoperatively compared with saline placebo. These findings suggest the potential of MSC-derived secretome as a cell-free biological adjunct to improve patient-reported knee function and reduce postoperative pain following ACL reconstruction, warranting further evaluation in larger clinical trials.

title: Effect Of Joint-Angle Configuration on Hamstring Torque-Duration Relationship Parameters and the Etiology of Motor Performance Fatigue.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study examined how hamstring muscle-tendon unit length influences critical torque (CT), work capacity above CT (W'), and the mechanisms of motor performance fatigue during and after repeated maximal voluntary contractions.
METHODS: Twelve healthy men (25 ± 4 years) performed, on separate days, two fatiguing protocols consisting of fifty 3-s maximal isometric knee flexions (2-s rest) at joint-angle configurations expected to produce relatively long (LL) and short (SL) hamstring muscle-tendon unit lengths. Neuromuscular assessments were conducted before, during, and up to 15 min post-exercise. CT and W' were determined from the torque-duration relationship. Peripheral fatigue was evaluated using peak evoked torques (T100), and central fatigue using voluntary activation (VA) derived from the twitch interpolation technique. Linear mixed-effects models and paired t-tests assessed the effects of time and joint-angle configuration.
RESULTS: CT did not differ between LL and SL (p = 0.65), whereas W' was significantly lower at SL than LL (p < 0.001, d = 0.96). MVC torque decreased by ~45% after fatiguing protocols (p < 0.001, η 2p = 0.84), accompanied by reductions in T100 (-22%) and VA (-17). During recovery, VA returned to baseline within 3 min, while T100 remained depressed throughout recovery (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In the knee flexors, short muscle-tendon unit length reduces the capacity to perform work above CT without altering CT or the magnitude and etiology of fatigue. The rapid recovery of voluntary activation alongside persistent peripheral impairment extends current knowledge of recovery kinetics specifically for repeated maximal knee-flexion exercise.

title: Chinese ethnic traditional sports as mind-body interventions for psychiatric recovery.
abstract: Chinese ethnic traditional sports (CETS)-a family of culturally embedded physical practices encompassing traditional Chinese mind-body exercises (e.g., Tai Chi, Qigong, Baduanjin, Yijin Jing, Wuqinxi) and intangible cultural heritage folk sports (e.g., dragon-lion dance)-have attracted growing interest as accessible, low-cost mind-body interventions for mental health. This narrative review examines which mental health outcomes are associated with participation in different types of CETS and to what extent the available evidence supports their role in psychiatric recovery. The review synthesizes 68 studies published between January 2000 and June 2026, identified through multi-database searches of Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus. Thematic synthesis identified four interconnected dimensions of mental health burden addressed by CETS: (a) affective disorders; (b) trauma-related disorders; (c) sleep-wake disturbances; and (d) cognitive and psychosocial dysfunction. Across these dimensions, individual randomized controlled trials consistently report moderate reductions in depressive and anxiety symptoms, with larger effects when CETS are delivered in supervised groups at moderate intensity for 12-24 weeks; however, most evidence derives from subclinical or non-psychiatric samples and measures symptom severity rather than functional recovery. The review therefore concludes that CETS are a promising, low-cost, culturally congruent adjunct to conventional psychiatric care-warranting rigorous, disorder-specific trials-rather than established stand-alone treatments for psychiatric recovery.

title: Effects of Morning Strength and Power Priming Exercises on Afternoon Physical and Cognitive Performance in Male Rugby Union Players.
abstract: The objective of this study was to assess the effect of morning strength and power priming exercises on afternoon physical and cognitive performance in male rugby union players. On two occasions in a randomised, counterbalanced design, 25 male rugby union players completed morning physical (countermovement jump, 40 m linear sprint) and cognitive (rapid visual information processing; spatial working memory; paired associates of learning) assessments. Control (passive rest) or intervention (barbell back squat, 3 × 3 repetitions at 85% of one repetition maximum and barbell squat jump, 5 × 3 repetitions at 40% one repetition maximum) trials were implemented 5.5 h before afternoon assessments. Differences between morning and afternoon assessments were found in sprinting performance following intervention for 30 m fly (-0.08 ± 0.13 s, p = 0.004, ES: 0.615) and 40 m (-0.12 ± 0.17 s, p = 0.001, ES: 0.711) relative to control (0.03 ± 0.07 s, p = 0.022, ES: -0.476; 0.01 ± 0.09 s, p = 0.740, ES: -0.065, 30 m fly and 40 m, respectively). Afternoon countermovement jump flight time improved following intervention compared with control (2% vs. 0%, p = 0.012, ES: -0.53). No changes were found for cognitive assessments (p > 0.05). Morning strength and power priming exercises combining heavy-load traditional and light-load ballistic exercises effectively enhanced vertical jump and sprint performance, but not cognitive performance, in the afternoon in male rugby union players.

title: Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation and exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis: A mixed-methods pilot randomised controlled trial.
abstract: This mixed-methods pilot trial evaluated the feasibility and patient perceptions of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. Twenty-four participants were allocated to active or sham home-based tDCS plus exercise. Participants completed 10 tDCS sessions over two weeks and an eight-week exercise program, with laboratory assessments at baseline, week four, and week eight. Primary outcomes were recruitment, adherence, adverse events, attrition, and tolerability. Secondary outcomes included local pressure pain thresholds, pain, function, quality of life, and semi-structured interviews exploring intervention facilitators and barriers. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data using inductive thematic analysis. All prespecified feasibility and safety criteria were met. Adherence was high, with 88% of participants (21/24) completing at least 75% of tDCS sessions, and 75% (18/24) completing at least 75% of exercise sessions. No significant adverse events occurred. Mean (SD) pain intensity /100 decreased from 47.3 (25.6) to 28.3 (16.1) in the active group and from 46.4 (17.8) to 33.5 (16.7) in the sham group at week 8. A future trial would require 80 participants. Qualitative themes indicated that evidence of effectiveness was more important to engagement than financial cost, tDCS was viewed as an appealing alternative to pharmacological treatment, and initial device operation was a greater barrier than safety or home use. Home-based tDCS combined with exercise was feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable intervention improves pain and function in people with knee osteoarthritis. PERSPECTIVE: This pilot trial indicates that home-based tDCS combined with exercise is feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated for knee osteoarthritis. Participants valued its convenience and non-pharmacological nature. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable approach improves pain and function and broadens access to care.

title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
abstract: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

title: Updates on Low Energy Availability in Athletes: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and the Female or Male Athlete Triad.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This paper evaluates the latest literature on low energy availability (LEA) in athletes, which is the basis for the clinical conditions known as the Female Athlete Triad, Male Athlete Triad, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). It explores how these different conditions are related, and how the clinician can approach screening, diagnosis, and management of LEA in athletes.
RECENT FINDINGS: Within the past five years the Male Athlete Triad Consensus Statements were published in 2021, expanding upon knowledge regarding LEA in the Female Athlete Triad and applying this to the male population. Additionally, there has been an important update to the REDs model and a new clinical assessment tool (CAT2) published in 2023. This is based on new research into the different physiologic and psychologic sequelae of LEA. This has sparked additional discussion regarding the diagnosis, management, and prevention of LEA. The consequences of LEA can be severe, and can affect multiple different organ systems. Treatment should ideally involve a multidisciplinary team consisting of a physician, dietitian, and mental health provider, but may also include additional professionals such as athletic trainers, physical therapists, physiologists, other medical specialists, or other members of the athlete support system (including family and coaches). The mainstay of management remains optimizing energy availability (EA) through improving macro and micronutrient intake, and also requires addressing some of the more common sequelae of LEA. Prevention largely focuses on educational efforts and fostering healthy environments, particularly when discussing weight, body composition, and performance.

title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation.
METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization.
CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, expert opinion.

title: Task Force 5: Clinical Considerations for Myocarditis and Selected Cardiovascular Conditions, Including Valvular Heart Disease.
abstract: Athletes with myocarditis, pericarditis, valvular heart disease, and other acquired cardiovascular conditions require careful evaluation when considering competitive sports participation. This document outlines key clinical considerations, risk factors, and expert consensus, serving as the rationale for Section V of the recent AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are essential in determining return-to-play eligibility. This Task Force document addresses myocarditis, pericarditis, the cardiovascular impact of respiratory viral infections, incidental myocardial fibrosis, Kawasaki disease, infiltrative cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease.

title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

title: Strength Training in Youth: A Scoping Review with Evidence Gap Map.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Strength training has gained increasing attention in youth athletic development due to its benefits in performance and motor competence. However, a comprehensive overview of the literature examining strength training in youth populations is lacking, and research remains fragmented across sex, maturation stages, and intervention characteristics.
OBJECTIVE: To conduct a systematic scoping review with an evidence gap map of studies on strength training in youth aged 6-18 years to provide evidence-based priorities for future research and practice.
METHODS: This scoping review followed PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Studies involving youth athletes exposed to structured strength training interventions (e.g., resistance, bodyweight, or combined methods) were included. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus was conducted up to April 20th, 2025. Data were descriptively summarized using pre-defined themes and tabulation procedures, and an evidence gap map was generated to depict how research is distributed across training variables, outcome domains, and population characteristics.
RESULTS: Out of 3770 records screened, 342 studies were included. Approximately 90% of trials assessed physical performance outcomes (e.g., strength, power, sprint speed), with limited focus on motor competence, injury prevention, or psychosocial factors. Male participants dominated the sample pool, while sex-specific analyses were uncommon. Studies involving biologically mature adolescents were scarce, and intervention durations varied widely, with numerous studies extending beyond eight weeks. A substantial proportion of studies failed to adequately report key training variables, such as frequency, intensity, supervision methods, limiting replicability, and comparability. Strength training was primarily studied in team sport contexts, especially soccer and rugby, with individual sports under-represented. Psychosocial outcomes, contextual factors (e.g., training environment), and follow-up beyond 6 months were absent in most studies. Technological and innovative approaches, including velocity-based and flywheel training, were limited to pilot studies. The evidence gap map revealed critical deficiencies in female representation, long-term follow-up, biological maturation assessment, and multidimensional outcome evaluation.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence indicates that youth strength training has been widely studied in relation to physical performance, injury-related outcomes, and neuromuscular development. However, important evidence gaps remain regarding biological maturity, sex-specific responses, psychosocial outcomes, long-term follow-up and context-specific applications. This scoping review identifies these gaps and highlights key priorities for future research rather than providing definitive recommendations for training practice or policy.
