title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. Although most cases resolve with time, accurate diagnosis is essential to distinguish common musculoskeletal causes from more serious conditions. This article reviews key causes of athletic back pain, including muscle strain, mechanical low back pain, spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, lumbar disc herniation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

title: Clinical Assessments to Inform Return to Play Prognosis Following Acute Hamstring Injury: An Evidence-Informed Guide for Clinicians.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation clinicians aim to provide a return to play (RTP) prognosis following acute hamstring injury based on various clinical assessments, including subjective interview questions and physical examinations. CLINICAL QUESTION: What subjective interview questions and physical examinations should be prioritised during an initial clinical assessment following acute hamstring injury to inform RTP? KEY RESULTS: There are key subjective interview questions and physical examination findings to inform RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury. Prolonged RTP time has been associated with athletes who: 1) recall higher pain ratings at the time of injury; 2) report pain with palpation closer to the ischial tuberosity; 3) have greater cranio-caudal length of palpable pain; 4) present with between-leg deficits of greater magnitude in maximal hip flexion active knee extension range of motion and isometric knee flexion strength in outer-range (supine with 90° hip/knee flexion) and/or mid-range (prone with 0° hip and ~15° knee flexion); and 4) experience pain during outer-range hamstring contraction. CLINICAL APPLICATION: This evidence-informed clinical commentary may help clinicians prioritise subjective interview questions and physical examinations to inform their RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury.

title: Global Positioning System-Derived Match Demands and Their Association With On-Field Technical Performance in Elite Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) Athletes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study sought to determine the associations between global positioning system-derived match demands and technical performance in elite Australian Football League Women's athletes.
METHODS: Global positioning system match demands (total distance, speed, acceleration, high-intensity running [>19 km·h-1], very high-intensity running [>21 km·h-1], sprint distances [>24 km·h-1]) were measured with Catapult Vector S7 global positioning system units during the 2023 and 2024 seasons. Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes for each game were considered technical performance outcomes. Linear mixed effects regression models examined associations between match demands and technical performance, adjusting for season, ground location, and playing position.
RESULTS: Five hundred sixty-six player match profiles from 32 athletes across the 2 seasons were analyzed. Ranking points were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .29 [95% CI .22-.40]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.15]), and acceleration (R2 = .09 [.00-.23]). Best and fairest votes were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .23 [.17-.34]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.11]), acceleration (R2 = .05 [.00-.17]), and very high-intensity running distance per minute (R2 = .00 [.00-.13]).
CONCLUSIONS: Total distance, speed, acceleration, and very high-intensity running distance per minute were associated with Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes across Australian Football League Women's seasons 2023 and 2024. This suggests that athletes who cover greater total distances and achieve higher average acceleration get more opportunities to be involved in match-play and demonstrate higher levels of technical performance.

title: Comparative physiological responses to self-paced exercise in men across age-training status: effort distribution, cerebral-muscle oxygenation and neuromuscular performance.
abstract: To compare self-paced cycling performance, effort distribution, and associated neuromuscular and physiological responses across three age-training phenotypes. Twenty-eight healthy men were classified as young trained (YT, n = 8; 26.3 ± 6.9 y), older trained (OT, n = 11; 57.5 ± 3.4 y), or young untrained (YU, n = 9; 24.8 ± 5.3 y). Participants completed a 25-min self-paced cycling time trial comprising five 4.5-min lower-intensity sections, each followed by a 30-s maximal sprint. Power output, heart rate (HR), rating of perceived exertion, blood lactate, core and skin temperature, cerebral and muscle tissue oxygenation, and pre/post knee-extensor neuromuscular function were assessed. Total distance differed between groups (P = 0.037), with OT cycling further than YU (12.87 ± 1.32 vs. 11.48 ± 0.89 km; mean difference 1.40 km, 95% CI 0.35-2.44; adjusted P = 0.035), whereas OT and YT did not differ. During lower-intensity sections, OT produced greater absolute power than YU (mean difference 51.8 W, 95% CI 18.8-84.7; adjusted P = 0.012). Sprint-power variability was lower in OT than YU (7.8 ± 6.0 vs. 28.4 ± 18.5%; adjusted P = 0.030). Peak HR was lower in OT than both younger groups. Voluntary activation showed no significant group x time interaction (P = 0.062), and NIRS responses showed no significant group x stage interactions. Older trained men achieved self-paced cycling performance comparable with young trained men and greater than young untrained men, characterised by sustained lower-intensity power and more stable sprint output despite a lower peak HR.

title: Adaptive training load optimization for sprinters via offline reinforcement learning and multi-modal physiological feedback.
abstract: Elite sprint training requires daily adjustment of training load to balance performance adaptation and fatigue, yet physiological monitoring does not necessarily translate into a specific next-session prescription. This study formalizes daily sprint training prescription as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process and develops an adaptive load-optimization framework that couples multi-modal physiological feedback with offline reinforcement learning (RL). A 19-dimensional state fusing autonomic, neuromuscular, endocrine, subjective, and load-aggregate signals is encoded by a dual-tower network [a one-dimensional convolutional neural network-Transformer temporal branch and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) static branch] over an action space of 62 admissible training-type/intensity/volume combinations. A composite reward penalizes overreaching while rewarding short-term gain, longitudinal adaptation, and acute-to-chronic workload ratio conformity. The policy is learned by conservative off-policy training on retrospective data, evaluated through the Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and Doubly Robust (DR) estimators, and presented to coaches as the three leading candidate actions, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values used to explain the model's preferences among the candidate actions. In a 12-week single-center retrospective comparison of 70 national-level sprinters (35 men and 35 women; 100 m personal best (PB) ≤ 11.20 s for men or ≤ 12.50 s for women), grouped by whether their squad had adopted the tool (n = 35 RL-guided) or continued classical block periodisation (n = 35 control), the RL-guided cohort demonstrated between-cohort differences of +0.240 s in 100 m [95% confidence interval (CI) +0.128 to +0.352; p < 0.001, d = 1.00], +0.104 s in 30 m (p < 0.001, d = 1.00) and +2.17 cm in countermovement jump (p < 0.001, d = 1.01). Zero algorithmically defined sustained multi-indicator fatigue/load events were observed in the RL-guided cohort vs. seven in the control cohort (1.43 per 1,000 athlete-days); these events should not be interpreted as clinically diagnosed overtraining syndrome. Off-policy evaluation yielded exploratory point estimates whose precision remains unknown because uncertainty intervals were not calculated. These observational findings describe associations with an RL-guided, coach-in-the-loop workflow and do not establish a causal effect of the RL policy.

title: Collective case study on periodized training in elite female middle- and long-distance swimmers preparing for national competition.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elite swimmers increasingly face calendars requiring multiple performance peaks within a single season, a scenario for which traditional single-target periodization models may be insufficient.
METHODS: This longitudinal collective case study followed five elite female middle- and long-distance freestyle swimmers across a 52-week macrocycle preparing for two national championships. The program combined three altitude camps, sea-level integration phases and two timed tapers. Training intensity distribution (TID) was quantified with a three-zone lactate-threshold model; hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, creatine kinase and cortisol were measured at four time points; and performance was assessed by time-trial and official competition results. Given N = 5, analysis prioritized a smallest-worthwhile-change (SWC) classification for performance and paired effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for blood markers rather than null-hypothesis significance testing. Hematological outcomes are concentration-based indices; training-load descriptors refer to in-water swimming only.
RESULTS: Applying an SWC of ≈0.24% to the 20 athlete-by-event observations, 12/20 (60%) changes at Competition 1 and 18/20 (90%) at Competition 2 exceeded the SWC, most representing improvement over baseline; this ordering held across the full defensible range of reference variability (SWC 0.22-0.42%). Hematological effect sizes were largest at Week 27 (RBC: Hedges' g = 2.32, 95% CI [0.64, 4.01]; HCT: g = 2.04 [0.50, 3.58]), while creatine kinase and cortisol peaked at Week 17 and were closer to baseline at Week 49, compatible with a lower physiological stress state at that sampled time point. TID shifted across phases (pyramidal during base development, polarized during altitude blocks, threshold-oriented during race-pace sharpening), with marked inter-individual heterogeneity in performance and physiological responses.
CONCLUSION: Across this double-peak macrocycle, most athlete-by-event changes exceeded the SWC, and the proportion doing so was higher at the second championship than at the first; these changes occurred alongside altitude-associated increases in concentration-based oxygen-transport indices and a taper-associated normalization of creatine kinase and cortisol. With no control group or randomization, only five athletes and four blood samples, several simultaneous interventions and unmeasured confounders (iron status, menstrual-cycle phase, dryland load), these findings describe associations only. They are offered as exploratory, hypothesis-generating observations from a single elite squad rather than as causal evidence.

title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

title: Associations between countermovement jump impulse and running kinetics following ACL reconstruction.
abstract: Persistent deficits in lower-limb loading are commonly observed following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and may influence running biomechanics. Countermovement jump (CMJ) impulse can provide a phase-specific measure of force-time characteristics to reflect limb loading capacity; however, its relationship with running kinetics remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify phase-specific CMJ impulse following ACLR and examine associations with vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) metrics during treadmill running at the return-to-running phase. Forty-two participants performed three unilateral and bilateral CMJs on dual force plates and ran at 8 km/hr on an instrumented treadmill. Concentric, eccentric braking, and landing impulses were calculated. Running variables included weight acceptance rate, weight acceptance peak force, and maximum applied force. Inter-limb differences were assessed using Wilcoxon/paired t-tests. Impulse-vGRF relationships were analysed using Pearson/Spearman correlations and multiple linear regression. The ACLR limb exhibited significant deficits across all unilateral and bilateral CMJ phases, except for unilateral landing impulse. Deficits were greatest for unilateral concentric impulse (Δ1.3Ns·kg-0.67, d = 1.49, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force limb symmetry index (LSI) was explained by unilateral concentric impulse LSI (adjusted R2 = 0.25, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric impulse (adjusted R2 = 0.38, p < 0.001). Weight acceptance peak force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric and landing impulses (adjusted R2 = 0.37, p < 0.001). No meaningful relationships were observed for eccentric impulses or weight acceptance rate metrics. These findings indicate that jump impulse testing may provide clinically relevant indicators of running kinetics.

title: Nationwide Trends, Regional Variation and Seasonality of Surgically Treated Achilles Tendon Rupture in Japan: An Analysis of Descriptive Epidemiological Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a common foot and ankle injury among physically active adults. Nationwide evidence on long-term trends, regional variation, seasonality and COVID-19-related changes in Japan is limited. We characterised the surgical burden of ATR using a national administrative database.
METHODS: We conducted a nationwide descriptive epidemiological study using aggregated data from the National Database of Health Insurance Claims and Specific Health Checkups (NDB) Open Data for fiscal years (FY) 2014-2022. Temporal trends, prefectural variation, seasonal patterns and pandemic-associated changes were examined using counts, population-based rates and quasi-Poisson regression.
RESULTS: During FY2014-2019, approximately 11,200 surgeries were performed annually (8.8 per 100,000 person). In FY2020, incidence declined to 5.9 per 100,000 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.67), with greater reductions among adults aged 30-59 (61%-64% of baseline) and, after age adjustment, among women (IRR 0.61 vs. 0.71 in men; interaction p = 0.039). Incidence partially recovered in FY2021-2022 (7.6 per 100,000; IRR 0.86). Incidence varied across the 47 prefectures (pre-COVID range: 5.0-16.7 per 100,000), and all declined in FY2020 (mean ratio 0.69). Monthly counts peaked in spring-early summer and were higher in spring than in winter (p = 0.018).
CONCLUSIONS: The incidence of surgically treated ATR in Japan was stable before the COVID-19 pandemic, declined markedly in FY2020 and partially recovered thereafter, with the largest reductions among working-age adults and women. Regional variation and seasonality were preserved. These findings can inform surgical and rehabilitation service planning.

title: Time-Efficient Reactive Agility Training Improves Motor and Cognitive Components of Reactive Agility in Open- and Closed-Skill Athletes: A 6-Week Intervention Study.
abstract: Reactive agility (RA), the ability to respond to external stimuli with whole-body movements as quickly and precisely as possible, is crucial for many sports, particularly open-skill sports, and is influenced by both motor and cognitive abilities. This study aims to investigate which of the underlying components of RA is most improved through RA training, whether prior experience with RA movements influences the rate of improvement, and whether a time-ecological approach also leads to improvements. Assessments included 19 open-skill and 26 closed-skill athletes with different competitive backgrounds. RA training was carried out once a week for six weeks with each session lasting 20 minutes. Pre- and post-assessments were conducted for RA (Random Star Run), change-of-direction (t-Test), and cognitive performance (Stroop test). Baseline differences between open- and closed-skill athletes and performance level were evaluated using 2 × 2 ANOVA. Intervention effects were calculated using repeated measures ANOVA. Open-skill athletes were significantly faster within the RA task than closed-skill athletes (p = 0.017; F = 6.247; η2 p = 0.132). Both groups improved significantly across all outcome measures (p < 0.05; RA and both underlying properties) with no interaction effects of group × time (p > 0.05). One weekly 20-min training session is sufficient to improve RA, and selected motor and cognitive performance parameters. Prior experience, based on regular participation in open-skill sports, seems to be associated with higher RA performance but does not moderate training adaptations, as both groups improved similarly in RA and the underlying motor and cognitive functions.

title: Mechanisms and Movement Patterns of Ankle Sprain Injuries in Male Handball: A Video-Based Analysis.
abstract: Ankle sprains are among the most common injuries in handball. However, evidence on high-risk movements and injury circumstances is scarce. This video analysis study investigated the situational characteristics of athletes sustaining ankle sprains. A systematic web search (YouTube, Google News) identifying video recordings of ankle injuries in male handball players was performed. Two independent examiners extracted sample information (e.g., age, height, weight, position), mechanism of injury (direct, indirect, non-contact), movement pattern (landing, change of direction/CoD, running, shuffle, step/lunge, other), action speed, focus of visual attention, and time of injury. In addition to descriptive statistics, χ2-tests were used to examine variable associations. A total of 118 video-recorded injuries were obtained. Most sprains were direct contact injuries (n = 72, 61.0%), and the most frequent movement patterns were landing (n = 46), running (n = 15), step/lunge (n = 14), and CoD (n = 13). While direct injuries occurred primarily during landing (43%), non-contact mechanisms (85%) were, by far, the main cause of injury during change of Direction movements (p < 0.01). In the majority of cases, movement speed was moderate (n = 63) and visual attention was directed to the ball (n = 56). Landings are the most frequent cause of ankle sprains in male handball players. Although the largest share, particularly landing-related injuries, results from direct contact, non-contact sprains display a unique pattern as they mostly occur during CoD. Conditioning coaches and health personnel may consider this disparity when designing preventive measures.

title: Tired of Thinking? Think Again! A Longitudinal Experience-Sampling Study of Bidirectional Dynamics Between Rumination and Mental Fatigue in Athletes.
abstract: Recovery days are intended to support psychological and physical recovery, yet repetitive sport-related thinking may interfere with this process. This four-week experience-sampling study examined the dynamic interplay between rumination and mental fatigue during rest days in competitive athletes, as well as the moderating roles of perfectionistic concerns and perfectionistic strivings. A total of 134 athletes completed repeated rest-day assessments of rumination and mental fatigue, with perfectionism measured at baseline using a sport-adapted version of the FMPS-Brief. Continuous-time structural equation modelling revealed significant bidirectional coupling between rumination and mental fatigue, supporting a self-reinforcing dynamic in which rumination fuels fatigue, and accumulated fatigue heightens the likelihood of further rumination, creating a 'vicious cycle'. The rumination → mental fatigue pathway was stronger than the reverse, underscoring the critical importance of mental rest and psychological recovery in sport. Perfectionistic concerns significantly moderated this association, suggesting that athletes high in evaluative self-criticism may be more vulnerable to the rumination-fatigue cycle, whereas perfectionistic strivings did not exert a moderating effect. These findings advance a process-oriented understanding of psychological recovery in athletes and may inform future research on how short-term rumination-fatigue dynamics contribute to longer-term maladaptive recovery patterns, including burnout risk. Interventions targeting repetitive negative thinking, such as mindfulness-, cognitive-behavioral-, or acceptance-based approaches, may help athletes preserve psychological recovery under performance demands.

title: Age-related slowing of sensorimotor reaction time in masters track and field athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Masters athletes offer a powerful model for understanding how lifelong training shapes age‑related changes in reaction time (RT), a key indicator of sensorimotor performance.
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional study examined RT in masters track and field athletes across age, sex, RT tasks of varying complexity, and event disciplines (endurance, power, sprint).
METHODS: A total of 182 competitors (82 females) from the 2025 World Masters Athletics Championships completed four RT tasks using a wireless light-based testing system.
RESULTS: RT increased progressively with age across all tasks, with the slowest responses consistently observed in athletes ≥80 years old. Female athletes demonstrated slower RT than males, and RT increased systematically with task complexity. Sprint athletes showed faster RT than endurance athletes overall, although event‑specific differences did not persist within age groups. Age was positively associated with RT in all tasks (r = 0.41-0.53), with similar correlation strengths between sexes. Quadratic age effects emerged selectively in male athletes for two-hand simple and step-choice tasks, suggesting accelerated slowing at older ages in tasks requiring greater motor coordination. Linear regression models indicated that RT increased by approximately 3.3-3.6 ms per year of age after adjusting for sex, task, and event discipline, while body composition variables were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Although lifelong training is associated with better sensorimotor performance, slower RT remains evident in masters athletes, with consistent sex differences and minimal influence of event discipline.

title: More than a shot: function over pain with tele-supervised resistance exercise added to hyaluronic acid injection in knee osteoarthritis, a randomized add-on trial.
abstract: Exercise is central to knee osteoarthritis (KOA) care, and intra-articular hyaluronic acid (IAHA) is often used as an adjunct, yet access to supervised exercise after injection is limited. Whether adding tele-supervised resistance band exercise (TSBE) improves outcomes beyond IAHA alone is unclear. Eighty adults with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 1-3 KOA who had not responded adequately to conservative care received a single IAHA injection and were allocated to a 12-week TSBE or standard education without supervised exercise. The between-group difference in Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total change favoured TSBE (-5 points, 95% CI - 9.86 to -0.13; p = .044). TSBE also favoured WOMAC physical function (-4.88, 95% CI - 8.28 to -1.47), 30-second sit-to-stand (+3.79 repetitions, 95% CI 2.80 to 4.79), and timed up-and-go (-1.87 s, 95% CI - 2.34 to -1.41), but not VAS pain (-0.38, 95% CI - 1.00 to 0.25). Adding TSBE to IAHA improved function and mobility, with no additional reduction in pain.

title: Adjustment of the Anteroposterior Center-of-Pressure Position Reduces Asymmetrical Knee Loading During Double-Leg Squatting After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract: Asymmetrical knee extension moments (KEMs) are associated with poor clinical outcomes following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. However, effective corrective methods remain limited. Thirty-four individuals (144.1 [60.2] d postanterior cruciate ligament reconstruction) performed 12 sets of 5 squats with visual feedback to maintain a symmetrical anteroposterior center-of-pressure position. Limb symmetry indices were calculated for KEM, vertical ground reaction force, and knee-to-support moment ratio (knee moment divided by the sum of hip, knee, and ankle extension moments). A mixed-model analysis of variance examined the effects of group (asymmetry: baseline KEM limb symmetry indices < 90%; symmetry: ≥90%) and time (baseline, post-biofeedback). Biomechanical changes were observed primarily within the asymmetry group (21 participants), which showed increases in limb symmetry indices for KEM (73.0% [10.5%] vs 85.4% [15.5%], P < .001), knee-to-support moment ratio (81.0% [16.7%] vs 87.4% [14.8%], P = .006), and vertical ground reaction force (90.5% [7.1%] vs 96.3% [8.6%], P = .003). Notably, these differences were primarily driven by changes in the uninvolved limb rather than the involved limb. No significant changes were observed in the symmetry group. While biofeedback of the anteroposterior center-of-pressure position reduced asymmetrical knee loading, further strategies are required to specifically elicit changes in the involved limb.

title: Supervised Combined Exercise as an Intervention in Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Mixed-Methods Case Report.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) remains a severe clinical condition associated with persistent symptomatology, functional impairment, and unhealthy lifestyle patterns. This case report examines the effects of a supervised combined exercise intervention using a mixed-methods approach. A 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of TRD treated with clomipramine (150 mg/day), lamotrigine (400 mg/day), and bromazepam (3 mg/day) presented with moderate depressive symptoms (Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale [MADRS] = 28; Clinical Global Impressions Scale [CGI-S] = 4), marked sedentary behavior (approximately 13 h/day), low cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) (VO2peak = 18 mL·kg-1·min-1), and elevated fat mass (42%). She participated in a 12-week supervised combined exercise programme (aerobic and resistance training, twice weekly) within the TRACE-RMD framework. Following the intervention, depressive symptoms decreased by 57% (MADRS = 12), with remission of global illness severity (CGI-S = 1) and a 16.7% increase in CRF. Functional disability and perceived stress were substantially reduced, while perceived social support markedly increased, as assessed by the Sheehan Disability Inventory (the global score reflects disability, item 4 reflects perceived stress, and item 5 reflects social support). Qualitative narratives indicated improvements in mood regulation, reduced rumination, increased self-efficacy, and enhanced social reintegration. Supervised combined exercise may represent a feasible and clinically meaningful adjunctive intervention in TRD, acting not only on symptom reduction but also on functional recovery and psychosocial re-engagement. Further controlled studies are warranted.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov identifier (NCT05136027).

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: Increased patellar tendon size and stiffness are associated with reduced knee extensor rate of torque development after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with bone-patellar tendon-bone graft.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Knee extensor weakness persists long-term following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) with a bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft, yet the contribution of donor patellar tendon morphology and mechanical properties to these deficits remains unclear. The purpose of this study was to determine whether donor patellar tendon properties were associated with knee extensor rate of torque development (RTD) and peak torque following ACLR with BPTB autograft.
METHODS: Twenty-five individuals (18.4 ± 2.8 years) underwent ultrasonography of the patellar tendon and isometric knee extensor strength testing approximately 3-4.5 months postsurgery. B-mode ultrasound and shear wave elastography were collected bilaterally to assess patellar tendon cross-sectional area (CSA), thickness and regional stiffness.
RESULTS: The donor patellar tendon was significantly larger (p < 0.001), thicker (p < 0.001) and stiffer (p = 0.001) than the uninvolved tendon. Patellar tendon CSA, thickness and stiffness were not associated with peak torque (p = 0.146 to 0.853); however, several properties were identified as negative predictors of RTD. Medial patellar tendon stiffness was the strongest negative predictor of RTD (R 2 = 0.276, p = 0.007), with stiffness, CSA and thickness collectively explaining 40.8% of the variance in RTD (p = 0.010).
CONCLUSIONS: Patellar tendon adaptations after graft harvest were negatively associated with RTD but not peak torque. While not causally established, these findings provide a potential target for rehabilitation aimed at restoring explosive strength after ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Pelvic floor knowledge and unhealthy habits related in female athletes: a cross-sectional study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To describe pelvic floor (PF)-related knowledge and unhealthy habits among female athletes, and to examine their associations with PF dysfunction (PFD) symptoms, sports characteristics, academic level and help seeking attitudes.
METHODS: A total of 538 female athletes (36.7 ± 11.3 years) completed an anonymous online questionnaire covering age, academic level, sports experience, unhealthy PF-related habits, PFD symptoms, professional healthcare-seeking attitude and knowledge about urinary incontinence (UI), anorectal incontinence (ARI), pelvic organ prolapse (POP) and female sexual dysfunction (FSD). Adequate knowledge was considered as ≥70% correct responses.
RESULTS: Female athletes demonstrated adequate knowledge regarding UI, ARI and POP, but insufficient knowledge about FSD (52.6%). Several PFD symptoms were associated with lower knowledge levels and a higher number of unhealthy habits compared with athletes without these symptoms (p<0.05). Younger athletes showed lower knowledge about ARI (p=0.033) and POP (p=0.003), while older athletes showed lower knowledge about FSD (p<0.001). Athletes who rejected professional healthcare showed lower knowledge across all PFD domains (p<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Female athletes reporting symptoms suggestive of PFD showed lower levels of knowledge and a higher number of unhealthy PF habits compared with those without symptoms. Although athletes generally demonstrated an appropriate level of knowledge regarding PFD, important gaps were observed in the FSD domain and in unhealthy toileting and sport-related habits, particularly among athletes without university studies. Differences in knowledge were also observed according to age and healthcare-seeking attitudes, highlighting areas that may be considered in future educational initiatives.

title: Obturator internus muscle entrapment in posterior wall acetabular fractures: two cases with preoperative and intraoperative findings.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We report two cases of the rare presentation of obturator internus muscle (OI) entrapment in posterior wall fractures of the acetabulum. Although piriformis muscle entrapment has been previously reported, to the best of our knowledge, OI entrapment associated with posterior wall acetabular fractures has not been previously documented.
CASE PRESENTATION: Case 1: A 38-year-old male presented with right hip and knee pain following a road traffic accident. He was diagnosed with a posterior hip dislocation, posterior wall and posterior column fractures of the acetabulum, and a posterior knee dislocation. During surgery, the OI muscle was found interposed between the displaced posterior wall fragment and the remaining posterior column. Case 2: A 43-year-old male sustained blunt abdominal trauma and a Pipkin type IV injury involving a femoral head fracture associated with a posterior wall acetabular fracture following a road traffic accident. After stabilisation of the abdominal injury with laparoscopic repair of the mesenteric injury, the patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the posterior wall fracture, along with removal of intra-articular fragments associated with an infra-foveal femoral head fracture. Intraoperatively, the OI muscle was similarly found interposed between the displaced posterior wall fragment and the remaining posterior column. In both cases, retrospective review of the preoperative CT images demonstrated OI interposition corresponding to the intraoperative findings. Both patients followed a standard postoperative rehabilitation protocol. At the one-year follow-up, both patients had satisfactory clinical outcomes, with Merle d'Aubigné-Postel scores of 16 and 17 and Harris Hip Scores of 92.7 and 93 for Cases 1 and 2, respectively. Neither patient showed radiographic evidence of post-traumatic arthritis.
CONCLUSION: These cases highlight the importance of recognising OI muscle entrapment as a potential cause of difficulty in reducing posterior wall acetabular fractures. Careful evaluation of preoperative CT images, particularly using soft-tissue window settings, may facilitate the identification of OI interposition. Intraoperatively, failure to identify the OI tendon between the superior and inferior gemelli, when both are clearly identified, should raise suspicion of entrapment. Meticulous identification of soft-tissue structures may help achieve anatomical fracture reduction and successful fixation.

title: Immediate effect of verbal cues on ACL injury relevant Knee loading during 180° and 90° cutting maneuvers in female university soccer and basketball athletes.
abstract: Young female athletes possess a high risk of rupturing their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). High external peak knee abduction moments (pKAM) are a likely key risk factor for non-contact ACL injuries. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of performance-based movement feedback on pKAM during cutting maneuvers in female university athletes. Thirty-four female university soccer and basketball athletes completed preplanned 180° and 90° cutting trials while ground reaction forces and kinematics were simultaneously captured. Participants immediately received verbal cues targeting foot strike angle, foot progression angle, or trunk lean angle based on their performance. Athletes then repeated the trials post-feedback. Changes in pKAM between baseline and post-feedback trials were analyzed. Soccer and basketball athletes who received the FOOTstrike-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM for both cutting tasks (Soccer: 180°; -0.21 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.92; 90°; -0.28 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 1.16. Basketball: 180°; -0.07 Nm/kg, p = 0.02, d = 0.76; 90°; -0.30 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.82). The FOOTpro-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM during the 180° cut for soccer athletes (-0.10 Nm/kg, p = 0.01, d = 0.60), but not basketball. The TRUNKlean cue did not significantly affect pKAM for either sport. Individual feedback targeting forefoot landings and neutral foot progression angles can elicit immediate technique change and reduce ACL injury relevant knee loading during cutting maneuvers.

title: Case Study Insights Into Female World-Class and Elite Athletes' Training and Physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This article offers a structured overview of published case studies involving elite and world-class female Olympic athletes, highlighting the unique insights these studies provide into training characteristics, physiology, performance, and female-specific factors.
METHODS: Four databases were systematically searched for peer-reviewed case studies involving tiers 4 to 5 female Olympic athletes reporting individual-level data on training, physiological, and/or performance characteristics.
RESULTS: Thirty-eight studies describing 54 elite and world-class female athletes from 18 countries and 19 Olympic sports met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were published after 2017 (68%), originated from Europe (58%), and involved endurance sports (81%). Fifteen studies examined long-term athlete development, with observation periods ranging from 4 to 26 years. Fourteen studies reported annual training and physiological characteristics across 10 sports including training volume, intensity distribution, periodization, and physiological profiling. Four studies examined altitude training, 8 addressed competition demands, tapering, and precompetition strategies, and 8 focused on female-specific physiology, health, and performance, including energy availability, menstrual function, hormonal cycle monitoring and pregnancy, and postpartum return to sport.
CONCLUSION: Case studies provide unique athlete-centered insights into the complex interactions between training, physiology, health, and performance in elite female athletes. Collectively, they demonstrate that pathways to world-class performance are highly individualized, while generating hypotheses that complement group-based research. Future case studies should prioritize underrepresented sports, geographical regions, and female-specific topics to expand the diversity of performance environments and athlete populations represented in the literature.

title: Effects of Combined Sprint and Plyometric Training vs Plyometric Training only on Physical Fitness and Sport-Specific Performance in Male Pubertal Soccer Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint (ST) and plyometric training (PT) are well-established methods for improving physical fitness and sport-specific performance in youth athletes. However, the effects of their combination remain unclear.
AIM: This study investigated the effects of an 8-week combined ST and PT program (SPT), PT-only program, and active control (CG) on physical fitness and sport-specific performance in young male soccer players.
METHODS: Forty-six pubertal Tier 2 training and performance caliber, male soccer players (13.9-14.2 years; maturity offset = 0.18-0.78 years from peak height velocity) participated in the study. Training was conducted twice weekly (2 × 30 min) over 8 weeks and was integrated into regular soccer sessions. The SPT program consisted of a progressive sequence of plyometric exercises (countermovement, line, drop jumps, and single-leg jumps/push-offs), immediately followed by a prescribed 10-15-m sprint or change-of-direction (CoD) task. The PT group performed the same plyometric exercises and exercise order without the subsequent sprint or CoD component. Training loads were monitored using the OMNI 0-10 RPE scale. The CG continued their regular soccer-specific training. Assessments included dynamic balance, muscle strength (reactive strength) and power (standing long jump, countermovement jump, five-jump test), speed (10-m and 30-m linear sprints), CoD speed with and without the ball, and sport-specific performance (throw-in and standing-kick tests).
RESULTS: Significant group × time interactions were observed for most outcomes (p < 0.05), with partial eta-squared (ηp2) values ranging from 0.33 to 0.81. Significant interactions were found for dynamic balance (ηp2 = 0.66), reactive strength (ηp2 = 0.33), power (ηp2 = 0.65-0.81), 10-m sprint performance (ηp2 = 0.42), CoD speed (ηp2 = 0.44-0.45), and sport-specific performance (ηp2 = 0.73-0.78). Bonferroni-adjusted between-group comparisons indicated significant differences between SPT and PT for selected outcomes, including dynamic balance, power (five-jump and countermovement jump tests), speed (10-m sprint and 15-m CoD without the ball), and throw-in performance, whereas no significant SPT-PT differences were detected for the remaining outcomes. Significant pre-post-improvements were observed across the assessed outcomes in the SPT group, while PT also produced significant improvements in several measures and the CG showed limited or non-significant changes. Although both SPT and PT significantly improved 30-m sprint performance, the group × time interaction did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.060, ηp2 = 0.12).
CONCLUSIONS: An 8-week combined SPT intervention was associated with greater performance than PT alone for selected physical fitness and sport-specific outcomes, particularly dynamic balance, power and throw-in performance, in pubertal male Tier 2 soccer players. However, these benefits were outcome-specific and were not observed across all assessed measures.

title: 3D Biomechanics of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Football: What We Have Learned in the Last Five Years.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most impacting injuries in professional football. Understanding these injuries in their environment, and their biomechanical mechanism, is the bottleneck between injury surveillance and effective mechanism-informed prevention and rehabilitation. We reconstructed the three-dimensional kinematics of 33 cases of ACL injury sustained by elite male football players during official matches. The Model-Based Image-Matching technique was leveraged to obtain quantitative, detailed estimates of three-dimensional joint kinematics, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional bidimensional video analyses. This paper reviews and interprets findings derived from over five years of research on the topic from a novel perspective. At the knee level, ACL injury mechanics involved a sequence of multiplanar joint rotations; on the sagittal plane, knee flexion increased from initial contact to injury frame; on the frontal plane, a knee abduction (valgus) shift emerged; on the transverse plane, following ground contact, we observed a sequence of internal and then external rotation of the femur, relative to the tibia, occurring during loading acceptance. Expanding the analysis on total-body kinematics, marked inter-individual variability was observed across the studied cohort; while ACL failure exhibits consistent kinematic features at the knee level, the sequence of whole-body postures leading to injury appears to be context-dependent. Finally, we propose biomechanically informed approaches to injury mitigation, emphasizing the integration of sport-specific contextual determinants, perceptual and decision-making processes, challenging the traditional separation between technical coaching and injury prevention.

title: Return to sports after pediatric brain tumors: Time to move beyond survival.
abstract: Brain tumors are the second most common malignancy in children and adolescents and the leading cause of cancer-related death in this population. While survival rates have improved, survivors are at risk of neurocognitive, motor, and psychosocial sequelae due to both tumor location and treatments used. Participation in sport is increasingly recognized as beneficial for functional recovery, cardiorespiratory fitness, and overall well-being in children and adolescents treated for brain tumors. However, return to play (RTP) may pose some challenges, particularly in the presence of neurosurgical devices, cranial radiotherapy, or residual neurological deficits. This narrative clinical review summarizes current evidence on the risks of sport-related injuries in pediatric brain tumor patients and survivors, highlighting factors influencing vulnerability, including treatment history and specific sport characteristics. We propose a risk-based framework for RTP evaluation emphasizing individualized coordinated assessment by pediatric oncologists, neurosurgeons, and sports medicine specialists. Protective strategies are discussed, although evidence for concussion prevention remains limited. A safe RTP should be enhanced by the here-proposed structured evaluation, balancing safety with the physical, cognitive, and psychosocial benefits of active participation. This framework aims to support clinicians and families in facilitating safe and effective reintegration of pediatric brain tumor survivors into both recreational and competitive sports.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Editorial Commentary: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Requires the Right Patient, the Right Dose, and the Right Time.
abstract: Quadriceps weakness is a persistent challenge after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. When used as an adjunct to rehabilitation, neuromuscular electrical stimulation can aid in quadriceps strength recovery. However, optimizing the clinical application of neuromuscular electrical stimulation requires consideration of the right patient, the right dose, and the right time. Volitional activation failure can limit adequate voluntary loading of the quadriceps, particularly in the early postoperative period. Although the evidence supports early neuromuscular electrical stimulation use when activation deficits are most pronounced, treatment should be guided by resolution of underlying impairments rather than postoperative time alone.

title: Being treated as more than a diagnosis: A qualitative interview study exploring patients' experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance in the management of tendinopathy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tendinopathy rehabilitation often involves exercise therapy and patient education. However, limited research has explored how patients experience and assign meaning to the guidance through which such care is delivered.
OBJECTIVES: This study aims to explore how adults with tendinopathy experience and make sense of physiotherapeutic guidance in clinical practice.
STUDY DESIGN: This qualitative study adopted a hermeneutic approach and employed semi-structured interviews with 10 patients receiving treatment for tendinopathy across various anatomical regions to explore their experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance throughout treatment.
RESULTS: From the patients' responses, two major themes were identified: "Meaningful guidance is built through trust, recognition, and individualisation" and "Purposeful guidance helps patients understand and manage the condition". Three sub-themes surfaced within each theme, and similar topics were identified among the patients' responses.
CONCLUSIONS: Physiotherapeutic guidance appears to be meaningful when it integrates relational and functional processes. While trust, recognition, and individualisation support patients' engagement, clear explanations and structured guidance facilitate understanding and self-management in daily life.

title: Delayed Extensor Apparatus Reconstruction for Post-Burn Digital Extension Loss in a Pediatric Patient.
abstract: Late sequelae of pediatric hand burns may include occult damage to the digital extensor apparatus beneath healed scar tissue. The digital extensor apparatus is a complex anatomical system composed of interconnected components that function together to produce coordinated finger extension at interphalangeal joints. Injury to this system may remain clinically unrecognized during acute burn management and present later as isolated extension loss despite preserved joint suppleness. We report the case of a 10-year-old girl who presented 2 years after a flame burn involving the dorsum of the left hand with inability to actively extend the index and middle fingers. Clinical examination demonstrated absent active extension at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, whereas passive motion, sensation, and vascularity were preserved. Overlying skin was supple, though scarred and variably pigmented. Radiographs demonstrated mild proximal interphalangeal joint subluxation of the middle finger without other osseous abnormality. Surgical exploration revealed loss of functional continuity of the digital extensor apparatus distally. Delayed reconstruction was performed using an ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon graft to restore coordinated extension. Temporary axial K-wire immobilization was maintained for 2 weeks, followed by structured rehabilitation. At final follow-up, the patient achieved approximately 80% recovery of active extension, enabling writing and functional grasp. This case underscores the importance of early recognition of occult extensor apparatus damage following pediatric hand burns to prevent functional disability. However, delayed reconstruction can still yield meaningful functional recovery when joint mobility and neurovascular integrity are preserved.

title: Cortical button versus suture anchor fixation in distal biceps tendon repair: a comparison of objective four-plane strength and functional outcomes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare four-plane isometric strength, function and complications between cortical button and suture anchor fixation in distal biceps repair, and to explore the influence of surgical delay.
METHODS: Twenty-eight men (mean age, 44.2 years) underwent single-incision repair with a cortical button (n = 16) or suture anchors (n = 12) between 2020 and 2025. At a mean follow-up of 46 months, we assessed isometric strength in four planes with a hand-held dynamometer (relative to the uninjured side), range of motion, QuickDASH, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score (OES) and complications. A sensitivity analysis included only patients followed for ≥ 24 months.
RESULTS: Mean strength was 93.8% (flexion), 100.1% (extension), 90.3% (supination) and 97.2% (pronation; median, 94.2%); all planes except extension remained below the uninjured side (P ≤ 0.016). Strength did not differ between techniques in any plane, also in the sensitivity analysis. Functional scores were high in both groups, with small differences in favour of suture anchors that should be interpreted with caution (MEPS 100 vs. 95.0, P = 0.022; QuickDASH 1.3 vs. 5.5, P = 0.046; OES 47.4 vs. 43.4, P = 0.069). Repair after 21 days (n = 6; exploratory) was associated with weaker flexion (85.4% vs. 96.1%, P = 0.024). No reruptures occurred; three patients (10.7%) had transient neurapraxia.
CONCLUSION: No significant strength differences were found between techniques, although the small sample cannot exclude clinically relevant differences and fixation was confounded with treatment era. A small supination and flexion deficit persisted after both techniques.

title: Arthroscopic Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Iliotibial Band Autograft With Bone Block.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction is the first-line treatment for ACL injury, whereas existing autologous grafts each have inherent limitations. This study describes the use of an iliotibial band (ITB) graft with a bone block for ACL reconstruction, designed as a femoral bone block combined with tibial tendon configuration, which precisely matches the anatomical attachment and biomechanical loading characteristics of the native ACL. The surgery is performed through arthroscopic evaluation, harvesting and weaving of the ITB with a bone block, creation of femoral and tibial bone tunnels, and graft introduction and fixation. This graft features the advantage of easy harvesting of the ITB, whereas the femoral bone column allows for rapid bone-to-bone healing, enhances stability within the femoral tunnel, and reduces the risk of tunnel widening and femoral-sided rerupture. Tibial-sided tendon fixation avoids excessive tibial tunnel enlargement and simplifies surgical steps. Arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using the ITB with bone block is technically straightforward and provides high initial stability. It offers another graft option for both primary treatment of ACL injury and revision surgery after failed reconstructions and is particularly suitable for patients with multiple previous tendon harvests from the same knee or those requiring large-diameter grafts because of bone tunnel enlargement.

title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
abstract: Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

title: Understanding the Complexity of Athlete Sleep: A Systems Approach to Modelling the Athlete Sleep Environment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athlete sleep can be disrupted by sport- and non-sport-related factors. However, the interactions of these sleep-related factors are not well understood. Systems science approaches, such as causal loop diagramming (CLD), provide an opportunity to map these interactions. This project aimed to (1) develop a CLD of the athlete sleep system describing the interacting variables, (2) identify feedback loops and potential leverage points to optimise athlete sleep, and (3) demonstrate the applicability of a CLD to guide the development of a sleep monitoring framework.
METHODS: A systems-based model of athlete sleep was developed using CLD, informed by existing literature and refined through a consensus process involving ten subject matter experts (nine from Australia, one from the USA). The model was then interrogated using network analysis to identify key variables based on their position and connectivity within the system. These findings informed the development of a generic sleep monitoring framework.
RESULTS: The CLD comprised 48 variables and 120 relationships across four domains: travel demands, behavioural and lifestyle factors, athlete condition and readiness, and resourcing and scheduling constraints. Overall, 12 key variables were identified, with hours of travel, number of time zones crossed, dose of caffeine, and amount of resources or expenditure available being the most connected upstream variables. Level of pre-sleep arousal, sleep opportunity, travel fatigue, and level of performance received the greatest number of incoming relationships, representing points at which multiple pathways converge. Physical condition, level of performance, quality of diet, and importance of competition most frequently linked different quadrants of the system. These variables informed a three-tier monitoring framework capturing upstream determinants and downstream consequences of sleep.
CONCLUSIONS: According to the CLD, sleep health in athletes extends beyond an individual behaviour issue and is influenced by the structure and functioning of sport systems. Interactions among travel demands, physical readiness, behavioural and lifestyle factors, and organisational constraints sustain athlete sleep health over time. Consequently, meaningful improvements in sleep health are likely to arise from both system-level interventions and individual behaviour change strategies.

title: Treatment of clavicle fractures in adolescents.
abstract: Clavicle fractures constitute 10% to 15% of all fractures in adolescents. Historically, adolescent clavicle fractures have been treated non-operatively. Although recent data in the adult population has led to an increased rate of operative fixation in the adolescent population, a vast majority of these fractures in adolescents can be managed conservatively. This manuscript provides an overview of the current standard of care for clavicular fractures in adolescents in the context of sports medicine practices. To achieve this, a nonsystematic search of computerized databases of peer-reviewed articles was conducted, and a critical appraisal of existing literature was subsequently performed. Middle third clavicle fractures are by far the most common type and a vast majority of these fractures can be treated non-operatively with a sling given the robust healing and remodeling seen in adolescents. Lateral third fractures are far less common but may pose a risk for nonunion according to adult literature. Medial third fractures are the least common type and while they are typically non-displaced, patients with posteriorly displaced medial third fractures must have concomitant intrathoracic injury ruled out. Additionally, timing of the injury relative to competitive season could play a role in decision making as surgical fixation of clavicle fractures has been shown to yield faster return to play times.

title: Sexual dimorphism in morphological predictors of upper- and lower-limb strength in adult rugby players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sex differences in athletic performance extend beyond body size, encompassing morphology-strength relationships.
AIM: To analyse sex-specific associations between body size and composition (body mass, fat-free mass [FFM], and thigh volume) and strength (hand grip strength and isokinetic knee extensor and flexor strength) in adult rugby players.
SUBJECTS AND METHODS: 84 players (42 males) were assessed. Body composition was measured by air-displacement plethysmography, and thigh volume was estimated anthropometrically. Strength was measured by grip (kg) and isokinetic knee torque at 60°·s-1.
RESULTS: Males were taller (178.3 cm), heavier (82.7 kg), and stronger (hand grip: 48.2 kg; knee extensors: 252 N·m). Females had a higher fat percentage (24.2% vs. 14.1%) and lower strength. FFM was the best predictor of peak torque in males (r ≈ 0.69 to 0.74); body mass correlated best (r ≈ 0.45 to 0.50) with peak torque in females. The hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio was, on average, 0.56 in both sexes.
CONCLUSION: Strength determinants differ by sex in rugby players. FFM is the primary predictor of strength in males, whereas body mass is more relevant in females. These findings support the development of sex-specific training methods to optimise performance and potentially reduce injury risk.

title: Evaluation of Barbed Suture in Side-to-Side Tendon Transfer Technique Using a Cadaveric Model.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: To evaluate the biomechanical performance and efficiency of a barbed, knotless side-to-side (STS) tenorrhaphy versus a traditional running cross-stitch STS repair in a cadaveric tendon transfer model.
METHODS: Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons (index, middle, and ring) from 5 fresh-frozen male cadaveric forearms (mean age 52.2 years) were harvested and randomized into 2 groups (n = 12/group). Each pair underwent a 3-cm overlap STS tenorrhaphy with either cross-stitch with a 3-0 braided polyester (Ethibond) or barbed running grasping repair with 2-0 barbed monofilament PDS (Stratafix). After 200 preconditioning cycles at 0.5 Hz to 10% strain (≤30 N), constructs were pulled to failure at 1 mm/s. Primary outcomes were ultimate load and stiffness; secondary outcomes included force reduction after cyclic loading and operative time.
RESULTS: All failures occurred at the repair. Mean ultimate load was lower with barbed versus cross-stitch (111.4 ± 26.1 N vs 166.7 ± 34.4 N; P < .002); stiffness was also lower (8.0 ± 2.3 vs 11.9 ± 2.4 N/mm; P < .0006). Displacement at failure was similar (~19-20 mm). Force reduction with cyclic loading did not differ (39% ± 11% vs 34% ± 16%). Barbed repair time was 27.2% shorter (199 vs 272 seconds).
CONCLUSION: Both STS techniques demonstrated ultimate loads substantially greater than the 15 to 35 N forces reported during passive motion and early active postoperative flexor tendon rehabilitation protocols; however, barbed constructs were approximately 33% weaker and less stiff than cross-stitch repair despite reduced operative time. Although barbed STS repair may have utility in select situations, running cross-stitch repair remains the biomechanical benchmark, and further optimization and clinical validation of barbed constructs are needed before broader adoption.

title: Hydrogels as drug carriers for cartilage repair in osteoarthritis: Applications and challenges.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent chronic degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodelling, synovial inflammation, osteophyte formation, and loss of joint function, resulting in significant pain, disability, and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Despite advances in clinical management, current therapeutic strategies, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids, hyaluronic acid injections, and surgical interventions, primarily provide symptomatic relief and have limited ability to prevent disease progression or regenerate damaged cartilage. In recent years, hydrogel-based drug delivery systems have emerged as promising therapeutic platforms owing to their excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, injectability, high water content, and structural similarity to the native extracellular matrix. These properties enable hydrogels to serve as effective carriers for a wide range of therapeutic agents, including anti-inflammatory drugs, growth factors, nucleic acids, nanoparticles, exosomes, and stem cells, while providing sustained and localized drug release within the osteoarthritic joint. This review comprehensively discusses the pathophysiology of OA and highlights the major molecular signaling pathways involved in disease progression, including NF-κB, MAPK, Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, TGF-β, and JAK/STAT pathways. Furthermore, recent advances in natural, synthetic, hybrid, and stimuli-responsive hydrogels are critically examined, with particular emphasis on their applications in cartilage repair and targeted drug delivery. Emerging approaches involving nanotechnology-enabled hydrogels, gene delivery systems, stem cell-loaded constructs, and immunomodulatory biomaterials are also evaluated for their therapeutic potential and translational prospects. This review provides an integrated and up-to-date perspective on hydrogel-based strategies for cartilage regeneration and disease modification, highlighting their potential as next-generation therapeutic platforms for the long-term management of osteoarthritis.

title: Excessive COX-Prostaglandin Signaling Promotes Cellular Senescence and Impaired Skeletal Muscle Recovery in Aging.
abstract: The ability to recover skeletal muscle after periods of disuse declines with age leading to persistent deficits in strength and function that extend beyond muscle mass loss. Here, we investigated whether age-related alterations in lipid remodeling contribute to impairment in skeletal muscle recovery following disuse. Lipidomic and oxylipin profiling revealed that aged mouse muscle is characterized by sustained phosphatidylcholine and omega-6-dependent COX-prostaglandin signaling during early recovery from disuse atrophy. This persistent lipid mediator response was associated with increased senescence burden, fibrosis, and impaired functional recovery. Pharmacological suppression of COX signaling during reloading in aged mice reduced senescence markers, limited fibrosis, and improved muscle function independent of improved muscle size. Mechanistically, senescent induced macrophages produced COX-2-dependent PGE2 and impaired myotube size and fusion through paracrine signaling. Activation of EP2 signaling was sufficient to induce a senescent macrophage phenotype. Importantly, a similar age-associated dysregulation of oxylipin content was observed in older adults after limb immobilization, supporting the translational relevance of these findings. Together, our results identify sustained COX-prostaglandin signaling as a key feature of impaired skeletal muscle recovery with aging and suggest that targeted modulation of this pathway may improve muscle recovery in older individuals. title: Effects of Resveratrol Supplementation on Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) is a common consequence of high-intensity or unfamiliar physical activity and can lead to muscle soreness, inflammation, oxidative stress, and temporary loss of muscle function. Although various interventions have been explored to alleviate EIMD, resveratrol (RES), a natural polyphenolic compound found in grapes, berries, and other plants, has attracted attention due to its potential antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. This review aims to explore the effects of RES on EIMD in terms of its impact on muscle recovery, inflammation, and oxidative stress markers. This review synthesizes the results of preclinical and clinical studies and highlights the timing, dosage, and efficacy of exercise-associated RES. Although the results are promising, with several studies reporting reduced muscle damage and improved recovery, inconsistencies in RES administration timing, dosage, and bioavailability require further investigation. Understanding these factors is critical to optimizing the therapeutic potential of RES in both the exercise and clinical settings. Finally, the review summarizes the potential of RES as a safe and effective intervention for EIMD and implications for future research.
